name: createClient
description:
Creates a Defjs {@link DerivableClient} from option helpers.

Options apply in order: a later option overwrites an earlier one for the same setting, and interceptors accumulate. Prefer creating the client inside the request boundary when interceptors close over auth or tenants. Balancer state (sticky endpoint, ejections, load) and the retry budget belong to the client, so a client created per request starts them fresh. Creating the client once and deriving per-call values keeps both; passing one shared balancer to `withBalancer` keeps the balancer state only. Default HTTP/SSE fetch availability is checked when an operation invokes transport.

The returned factory is a function. Calling it with {@link RequestOptions} returns a {@link Client} value for one call and performs no I/O; see {@link DerivableClient} for how request fields are captured. The factory itself is also a `Client` and carries no request options, so it can be passed to an operation directly. The base configuration is shared by every client value and is not frozen at runtime. It is fixed by convention: nothing in the library changes it, and applications should not either. Standard option helpers copy the fixed records they own when they are applied. A custom {@link ClientOption} may still retain a reference.

exampleFiles.code:
import { createClient, withEndpoint } from "@defjs/core";

const client = createClient(withEndpoint("https://api.example.com"));

returns: A callable factory that carries the resolved base configuration.

overloads.signature: function createClient(...options: ClientOption[]): DerivableClient;

parameters.name: ...options
parameters.description: Client option helpers such as `withEndpoint`.

name: isNoCandidateCause
description:
Whether `cause` is {@link ERR_NO_CANDIDATE}, including a copy from another Core build.

Returns `true` when `cause` carries the non-enumerable
`Symbol.for("defjs.cause.no-endpoint")` brand. Other values return `false`.
Pass `fault.cause`; this does not unwrap faults.

overloads.signature: function isNoCandidateCause(cause: unknown): boolean;

name: outlierDetection
description:
Wraps a strategy with consecutive-failure ejection by time.
Five attributed failures eject an endpoint by default. The penalty is the
minimum penalty (1s by default) times the penalty level, so successive
ejections last 1s, 2s, 3s and so on; uniform positive jitter of up to 0.5
times the base is added, and the total caps at 60s. By default (`halfOpen:
false`), when the time is up the endpoint is selectable again for every
caller; setting `halfOpen: true` admits only one trial request at a time
after penalty expiry, restoring full traffic on success or immediately
re-ejecting on failure. As in gRPC outlier detection (gRFC A50) a success
never clears the penalty level: every ejection raises it by one and every ten
seconds without one lowers it by one, evaluated when the endpoint is next
used. An endpoint that accepts a connection and then drops it is therefore
ejected for longer each time, as long as its failures return faster than one
level decays.
Every classified failure code fails by default, including NET_TIMEOUT and
NET_BODY_INCOMPLETE, as Envoy's consecutive 5xx and gRPC outlier detection
count timeouts and resets; `isFailure` replaces that rule. An attempted
outcome without a code resets the streak; unattributed attempts leave it
unchanged. The outcome of an attempt that began before an
ejection, or while the endpoint was ejected, is ignored even if it arrives
after the endpoint is selectable again, so late results do not eject it anew.
The child receives the filtered candidates as `endpoints` and the unfiltered
`members`, so ejection does not look like a membership change to it.
`isHealthy`, when supplied, is the only health judgement and combines with
ejection by AND: it can keep an endpoint out, and `true` cannot let an ejected
endpoint in. If it rejects every endpoint that is not ejected, it is ignored
for that pick. If every endpoint is ejected (or waiting on an in-flight
half-open probe), the original current list is used (Finagle panic mode).
`maxEjectionPercent` defaults to `100` (no quota); lowering it caps how many
endpoints may be ejected simultaneously. All callbacks are synchronous; no
timer is created. Configuration is captured at construction.
History holds at least 256 endpoints, and at least the current list, shared
across endpoint lists. LRU clean or expired states are evicted first, then
partial failure sequences, then the oldest protected state only if every
retained endpoint is ejected. Temporary candidate exclusion does not itself
erase a penalty.

parameters.name: child
parameters.description: Selection strategy retaining its identity and state.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Captured thresholds and application callbacks.

name: p2cBalancer
description:
Samples candidates without replacement and selects the least loaded draw.

Defaults to two choices and PeakEwma load: decaying RTT times (pending + 1).
`load: "pending"` selects the fewest in-flight attempts in the sample. Ties
favor the first draw. `choiceCount` is at least 2, capped at 10.
`defaultRttMs` defaults to 30 and `decayMs` to 10000 (Linkerd). Pending is reserved when `pick` selects the endpoint, so
concurrent picks in one tick see each other, and releases at `end`, the
beginning of a peer response (tower CompleteOnResponse), or at `done` when no
response began. RTT is the real start-to-end duration for every transport,
including failures. Higher samples replace the estimate; lower samples blend
exponentially, as in tower PeakEwma. Idle estimates decay toward zero. A done
without end creates no sample. Health filtering is off by default; with
`outlierDetection: {}` it ejects quickly failing endpoints. There is no
synthetic failure penalty.
Unlike Envoy and gRPC A48, draws are without replacement.
Load history keeps at least 256 endpoints, and at least the current members, in
LRU order, evicting idle entries first; an in-flight entry is evicted only if
all retained entries are busy. Evicted endpoints restart from the configured
initial estimate.

overloads.signature: function p2cBalancer(options?: P2cOptions): Balancer;

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Captured load settings, optional health filtering.

name: pickFirstBalancer
description:
Sticky failover balancer. The default when a client sets no balancer.

Uses the first endpoint until `done` reports
`{ attempted: true, code: "NET_UNREACHABLE" }` or `NET_UNAVAILABLE` for the
endpoint that is still sticky. The next `pick` then moves
to the following endpoint and wraps to the first. Other results, including timeouts and
`attempted: false`, keep the current endpoint. Overlapping failures advance
one step: a `done` that finds the sticky endpoint already changed does nothing.

Order and the sticky endpoint follow `members`. When the sticky endpoint is
not among this pick's `endpoints`, as when a wrapper filters candidates, the
pick takes the next candidate after it in member order without moving it, so
a narrowed pick never changes where later calls go. Only a sticky endpoint missing from `members`
resets the order to the first.

`shuffle: true` assigns each endpoint a random sort key on first sight and
sticks to that order. Keys survive a shorter endpoint list. The default is
`false`. Shuffle history keeps at least 256 endpoints, and at least the
current members, in least-recently-used order; a forgotten endpoint gets a new
random key when it returns.

`failbackMs`, when set, returns to the first endpoint by time
alone: once the sticky endpoint has been away from the first for that long, the
next pick whose candidates include the first selects it and makes it sticky
again. Nothing judges whether the first endpoint has recovered. If it fails
again, the ordinary advance rule above moves on and the time starts anew.
Choose an interval longer than the time between picks, such as a reconnect
delay, or every pick returns to the first endpoint. No background timer is
created.

Every successful `pick` returns `done`. An empty candidate list returns
`[ERR_NO_CANDIDATE, undefined]`.

Health filtering is off by default. Supply `outlierDetection: {}` to enable
default ejection, or configure its thresholds and application health function.
returns: A new balancer. Each call has its own sticky endpoint.

overloads.signature: function pickFirstBalancer(options?: PickFirstOptions): Balancer;

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional shuffled order, failback interval, health filtering.

name: roundRobinBalancer
description:
Round-robin balancer, with nginx smooth weighting when `weights` is set.

Without `weights`, a counter starts at a random `uint32` and each `pick`
returns `endpoints[counter % length]`, then increments the counter modulo
2^32. With `weights`, each pick adds an endpoint's weight to its current
value, selects the highest value (earlier candidate on a tie), and subtracts
the total weight of this candidate list. Members left out of this pick's
candidates keep their current value, as nginx skips a peer that is down. A
missing weight is 1. Weights for endpoints not in the list are ignored.
Selection and the cleanup of current values for endpoints that left the
members take O(member count + candidate count) work per pick. Extreme weights
are scaled to avoid overflow; ratios below floating-point precision may round
to zero. Finite positive weights never produce a non-candidate selection.

Without `weights`, every pick advances the counter, including a pick made for
a retry or a stream reconnect. Without `outlierDetection`, and with calls
that run one after another, an endpoint that fails persistently therefore
receives more than 1/n of the first attempts. With exactly two endpoints and
retries enabled it receives all of them, so every call needs one retry.
Concurrent calls interleave their picks and break this pattern.

Health filtering is off by default, so successful picks omit `done`. Supply
`outlierDetection: {}` to enable it: five consecutive attributed failures then
eject an endpoint temporarily. An empty
candidate list returns `[ERR_NO_CANDIDATE, undefined]`.
returns: A new balancer. Each call has its own counter and weight state.

overloads.signature: function roundRobinBalancer(options?: RoundRobinOptions): Balancer;

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional positive finite weights, health filtering.

name: withBalancer
description:
Replaces the balancer that selects one candidate per call.

The object is stored by reference and is not copied. A later
`withBalancer` replaces it. `withEndpoint` does not. Without this
option, each client gets its own `pickFirstBalancer()`.
This helper only stores the instance. HTTP retries are configured separately
with {@link withRetry}; the balancer knows nothing about retry policy.

overloads.signature: function withBalancer(balancer: Balancer): ClientOption;

parameters.name: balancer
parameters.description: Balancer whose `pick` chooses one endpoint per call.

name: withCredentials
description:
Sets whether HTTP and SSE requests include credentials.

When `value` is `true`, Fetch uses `credentials: 'include'`, so cookies and other credentials are sent with cross-origin requests. When it is `false` or never set, `credentials` is left unset and Fetch uses its default. The WebSocket constructor does not receive this setting.

overloads.signature: function withCredentials(value: boolean): ClientOption;

parameters.name: value
parameters.description: When `true`, credentials are sent with cross-origin requests.

name: withEndpoint
description:
Replaces the candidate base URLs prepended to relative request paths.

The arguments are copied in order and later duplicates of the same string are
dropped. This does not validate URLs and does not change `balancer`.
A later `withEndpoint` replaces the list; it does not merge. Zero arguments
are legal and store `[]`. The default list is empty.

The selected endpoint's pathname is kept as a directory; its query and hash are discarded. For WebSocket operations, an `http:` base becomes `ws:` and `https:` becomes `wss:`.

A missing, relative, or invalid endpoint, or an illegal request path, fails with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` during building, before any interceptor or transport runs, even when an interceptor would short-circuit. HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket share this rule. The resolved request must keep the base origin and stay under its directory; C0 control characters (including tab, CR, and LF), backslashes, `?`, `#`, and directory escapes in a path are rejected. Scheme-like and protocol-relative forms are rejected even with leading spaces; a plain inner space is allowed and sent as `%20`. An interceptor's final `req.endpoint` is checked against its final `req.baseEndpoint` with the same rule, but it may deliberately replace the base with another valid absolute URL. Deterministic URL errors are never retried.

overloads.signature: function withEndpoint(...endpoints: string[]): ClientOption;

parameters.name: ...endpoints
parameters.description: Candidate base URLs. Invalid values fail when a call builds a request.

name: withHTTPHandle
description:
Replaces the Fetch-compatible function used for HTTP requests.

The default is the platform `fetch`. `fetchImpl` is a {@link FetchHandle}, so a test double does not need host extras such as `fetch.preconnect`. It only affects HTTP. SSE uses {@link withSSEHandle}.

overloads.signature: function withHTTPHandle(fetchImpl: FetchHandle): ClientOption;

parameters.name: fetchImpl
parameters.description:
`(input, init?) => Promise<Response>`. Not `typeof fetch`, so
a mock does not need host extras such as `preconnect`.

name: withHeaders
description:
Sets static default headers for HTTP and SSE requests built by this client.

WebSocket connections do not use them. The `HeadersInit` is copied into a `Headers` object when the option is applied. A later call replaces the earlier headers instead of merging.

Headers returned by a request builder replace a default of the same name. The first value for that name replaces the default, and later values of that name, from a `[name, value]` array or a `Headers` instance, are appended to it. A record value is one value: an array joins with a comma the JavaScript way. Other default names stay.

Per-request or computed credentials, such as a refreshed Bearer token or an HMAC signature, belong in an interceptor, because they need the serialized body or a refreshed credential.

overloads.signature: function withHeaders(headers: HeadersInit): ClientOption;

parameters.name: headers
parameters.description: `HeadersInit` bag cloned onto the client config.

name: withInterceptors
description:
Appends interceptors to the client interceptor chain.

Calling it again appends more; it never replaces earlier ones. The first registered interceptor is the outermost layer. HTTP, SSE, WebSocket, and operation interceptors can be mixed in one call. When an operation runs, its operation interceptors wrap the whole call and only the interceptors of its transport run inside it, each in their registration order. Each `{ kind, fn }` record is copied when the option is applied. `fn` keeps its identity. Changing the original record later does not change clients already created.

overloads.signature: function withInterceptors(...interceptors: Interceptor[]): ClientOption;

parameters.name: ...interceptors
parameters.description: Interceptors applied in registration order.

name: withQuerySerializer
description:
Replaces query encoding for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket requests.

`serializer(query)` receives the encoded wire object: aliases applied, `Date` as an ISO string, `bigint` as a string. Nested objects and arrays are kept as they are. It must return the query string without a leading `?`. The string is parsed into the request's `query`, so the request sends `query.toString()`, the URL Standard's application/x-www-form-urlencoded serialization: a space is `+`, `[` is `%5B`, and the bytes the function wrote are not kept.

It is not called when the request has no query. A builder that returns `URLSearchParams` skips it. Without this option, queries use `URLSearchParams`: arrays repeat keys and a nested object fails.

overloads.signature: function withQuerySerializer(serializer: QuerySerializer): ClientOption;

parameters.name: serializer
parameters.description: Function that turns an encoded query object into a string.

name: withRetry
description:
Enables retries for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket, with backoff and an optional policy function.

Retries are opt-in: without this option every call makes one attempt, and an HTTP call creates no retry budget. Calling it with no argument or `{}` enables the defaults: 3 retries after the first attempt, a 1000 ms delay that doubles per retry up to 30000 ms, and jitter of 0.2. The same options apply to every transport; see {@link RetryOptions} for the decision order after a failure and for what counts as a retryable failure on each one.

- HTTP retries a method in `methods` when the attempt got no response, got a status in `statusCodes` (429, 502, 503, or 504 by default), or ran out of `attemptTimeoutMs`. Each retry rebuilds the request, reruns the complete interceptor chain, and lets the balancer pick again from every endpoint, so a single endpoint is tried again after the delay. Local failures before Fetch starts are not retried. Retry eligibility checks every method actually sent by the attempt, after interceptor rewrites; with no transport invocation it uses the defined method. A `budget` limits how many retries the client can make.
- SSE retries a method in `methods` after a handshake network failure, a handshake status in `statusCodes` (429, 502, 503, or 504 by default), an attempt timeout, or a network error after the stream opened. Normal EOF ends the stream. The `retry:` field of the server replaces `delayMs`, and the next attempt sends `Last-Event-ID`. A successful handshake resets the count.
- WebSocket retries every close that `session.close()` did not request, including a connection that never opened and a heartbeat timeout. A successful `open` resets the count.
- A `ReadableStream` request body, a caller abort, a manual close, and fatal errors end the call without a retry and without calling `shouldRetry`.

Callers that need a time limit without retries use `withRetry({ maxRetries: 0, attemptTimeoutMs })`. The signal of the caller covers all attempts and waits. A later `withRetry` replaces the policy as a whole, and passing `undefined` is the same as passing `{}`; pass `{ maxRetries: 0 }` to turn retries off after enabling them. The `methods` and `statusCodes` arrays and the `budget` record are copied when the option is applied. A request option `retry` replaces this policy for one call, except `budget`, which stays with the client.

overloads.signature: function withRetry(options?: RetryOptions): ClientOption;

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Retry policy; omitted or `undefined` behaves like `{}`.

name: withSSEHandle
description:
Replaces the Fetch-compatible function used to open SSE event streams.

The default is the platform `fetch`. `fetchImpl` is a {@link FetchHandle}. It only affects SSE. HTTP uses {@link withHTTPHandle}.

overloads.signature: function withSSEHandle(fetchImpl: FetchHandle): ClientOption;

parameters.name: fetchImpl
parameters.description:
`(input, init?) => Promise<Response>`. Not `typeof fetch`, so
a mock does not need host extras such as `preconnect`.

name: withSSEOnInvalidEvent
description:
Observes SSE events that have no matching event struct or fail validation.

The handler may be async and is awaited. The callback receives:

```ts
{
  reason: 'missing-struct' | 'validation-failed'
  message: { id: string; event: string; data: string }
  cause?: unknown
  signal: AbortSignal
}
```

- The invalid event is **always dropped**; it is never delivered to the stream. The callback only observes it.
- The return value is ignored. An error thrown by the callback is swallowed and does not close the stream, unless `signal` has already aborted.
- `cause` is set for `validation-failed`. Without a handler the invalid event is dropped silently.

parameters.name: handler
parameters.description: Observer callback for invalid events.

name: withWebSocketBeforeConnect
description:
Runs a hook before the initial WebSocket connect and before every reconnect.

The hook type is:

```ts
(context: { attempt: number; signal: AbortSignal }) => void | Promise<void>
```

- `attempt` is `0` for the first connect and grows by one for each reconnect.
- Pass `signal` into token refreshes and other async work so cancelling the session stops them.
- If the hook throws, the attempt fails with an `EXT_HOOK_FAILED` fault.
- A `beforeConnect` in the request options replaces this one for that call.

parameters.name: beforeConnect
parameters.description: Hook receiving attempt index and abort signal.
parameters.type: ((context: { attempt: number; signal: AbortSignal; }) => void | Promise<void>) | undefined

name: withWebSocketHandle
description:
Replaces the WebSocket constructor used for socket connections.

The default is `globalThis.WebSocket`. `WebSocketImpl` is a {@link WebSocketHandleConstructor} that returns a {@link WebSocketHandle}. If no constructor is available, a WebSocket operation fails with an `ENV_UNSUPPORTED` fault.

parameters.name: WebSocketImpl
parameters.description: Constructor that returns a `WebSocketHandle`.

name: withWebSocketHeartbeat
description:
Enables WebSocket heartbeat messages with optional acknowledgement detection.

Passing `undefined` clears an earlier setting. Defjs defines no heartbeat format: `message` and `isAck` are yours. The option type is {@link WebSocketHeartbeatConfig}:

```ts
{
  intervalMs: number
  message: () => unknown
  isAck?: (message: unknown) => boolean
  timeoutMs?: number // only together with isAck
}
```

- Every `intervalMs`, `message()` is called and its result is sent through the endpoint's `outgoing` struct as JSON text. No message is sent when it returns `undefined`.
- With `timeoutMs`, an acknowledgement is expected after each heartbeat; the type requires `isAck` then. `isAck` receives the decoded incoming message; when it returns `true`, the timer is cleared and that message is **not** delivered to `receive`.
- If no acknowledgement arrives within `timeoutMs`, the connection counts as failed: it is closed and the attempt enters the `withRetry` flow as a close that `session.close()` did not request. Without a retry policy the session ends with an `error` whose `cause` is the heartbeat timeout. A missing acknowledgement is reported to the balancer as `NET_UNREACHABLE`. A heartbeat that cannot be sent because `message()` throws or the value is not JSON is a local failure: it ends the session, is not retried, and is not attributed to the endpoint.
- A `heartbeat` in the request options replaces this one for that call.
- `intervalMs`, `isAck`, `message`, and `timeoutMs` are copied when this option is applied. `message` and `isAck` keep their identity. A getter runs at that moment and its exception escapes `createClient`.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Heartbeat interval, payload, timeout, and ACK predicate.

name: withWebSocketProtocols
description:
Sets the WebSocket subprotocols offered during the handshake.

They are passed as the second argument to the `WebSocket` constructor only when the list is not empty, so the platform can run the RFC 6455 subprotocol negotiation. They matter only when the server requires a specific subprotocol, for example `['json']` or `['v1']`.

Precedence, highest first: the `protocols` request option, this client option, then `protocols` on the endpoint definition. The array is copied when this option is applied, so a later edit of the original array does not retarget the client. Applying the same option to another client copies the array again.

parameters.name: protocols
parameters.description: Subprotocol list for the WebSocket constructor.

name: BuilderInput
description:
Parsed endpoint input that a request builder receives.

Object nodes are intersected with the internal `TaggedObject` brand, so they carry the struct that
produced them and alias, `Date`, and `bigint` encoding follow the value into
the request. Record entries and tuple items are branded the same way. At
runtime a record container is also tagged when the parsed value is an object,
whether or not it was merged. Array and tuple containers are not. `null` and
`undefined` are never tagged. Nullish modifiers recover the struct they
wrapped. Union options are distributed; intersection options are combined.
Any other struct falls back to `Infer<S>`.

`TaggedStructOutput` and `TaggedObject` are internal helper types.

overloads.signature: type BuilderInput<S> = TaggedStructOutput<S>;

name: DecodedResponse
description:
Response metadata plus a body that decoded against a declared struct.

Holding this type is the proof that decoding happened; a failed decode is
reported as a fault carrying `HttpMeta` alone.

overloads.signature: type DecodedResponse<TBody> = HttpMeta & { readonly body: TBody };

name: HttpAwaitResult
description:
Await-result tuple for an HTTP call: success is `[null, data, response]`, and failure is `[err, undefined, undefined]`.

`TData` and `TErrorData` are decoded body types. On success the third slot
carries `body` only when `output` was declared. On failure it is `undefined`,
because the fault already holds whatever response metadata existed.

overloads.signature:
type HttpAwaitResult<TData = undefined, TErrorData = undefined> =
  | [
      err: null,
      result: TData,
      response: [TData] extends [undefined] ? HttpMeta : DecodedResponse<TData>,
    ]
  | [err: FaultOf<TErrorData>, result: undefined, response: undefined];

name: HttpExecuteOptions
description:
HTTP fields read from {@link RequestOptions} for one call.

Progress callbacks, `retry`, and `signal`. There is no `timeout` or `abort`.

overloads.signature: type HttpExecuteOptions = UseRequestConfig;

name: HttpMeta
description:
Response metadata, available whenever a response reached the client.

It carries no `body`: a body only exists once a declared struct decoded it.

name: HttpProgressEvent
description:
Progress snapshot passed to upload and download callbacks.

Mirrors the `ProgressEvent` fields `loaded`, `total`, and `lengthComputable`.
`loaded` counts bytes read from the upload or download stream, not bytes
acknowledged by the server. Download bytes may already be decompressed.
Unknown lengths use `total: 0` and `lengthComputable: false`. A download total
is computable only with a positive `Content-Length` and an absent or
`identity` `Content-Encoding`; compressed downloads, other encoded responses,
and bytes exceeding `Content-Length` have an unknown decoded length. A
streamed upload also has an unknown total unless a valid explicit
`Content-Length` supplies it.

name: HttpProgressFn
description:
Callback invoked as request bytes are uploaded or response bytes are downloaded.

Passed as `onDownloadProgress` or `onUploadProgress` in `HttpExecuteOptions`.
Callbacks may be async and are awaited before the next chunk is processed. A
callback that throws or rejects fails the call with `EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`,
with the thrown value as `cause`, for downloads and uploads alike. Caller
cancellation still takes precedence and reports `NET_ABORTED`, or `NET_TIMEOUT`
when the abort reason is a timeout.

`onUploadProgress` reports progress only when the request body is a
`ReadableStream` that the caller passes. Any other body (`Blob`, `File`,
`ArrayBuffer`, `FormData`, a string, or `URLSearchParams`) is sent as built and
`onUploadProgress` is not called, on every runtime. The library never converts
a body into a stream. Download progress is unaffected.

A `ReadableStream` request body follows the Fetch rules for streaming request
bodies, with or without `onUploadProgress`:

- Chromium and WebKit accept a streaming request body only over HTTP/2 or
  later, so the call fails with `NET_UNREACHABLE` on HTTP/1.1, with a
  runtime-specific `TypeError` as `cause`. WebKit was checked manually at 27.2
  only; this repository does not test it. Node.js and Bun accept HTTP/1.1,
  which departs from the Fetch standard.
- Firefox cannot stream request bodies, so the call fails with
  `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`.
- In browsers, a cross-origin request needs a CORS preflight, unless the
  browser holds a cached preflight result, and fails unless the server
  answers `OPTIONS`. A same-origin request is not preflighted.
- A 301, 302, 307, or 308 redirect fails after the body was sent once. A 303
  redirect becomes a GET and succeeds.

`fetch` gives the same network error for each of these as for an unreachable
endpoint, and for a source `ReadableStream` that throws while `fetch` reads
it, so the error does not reliably show the endpoint is down. The load
balancer therefore receives `{ attempted: false }` for it, as it does for a
throwing progress callback (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`). A healthy endpoint is not
ejected for these failures, but a down endpoint is not detected by streamed
uploads alone, and a rejected streamed upload is never retried: a
`ReadableStream` body ends the retry flow before `shouldRetry` is asked.

A streamed body has no known length, so the reported `total` is `0` and
`lengthComputable` is `false` unless the request carries a valid
`Content-Length` header. That header only sets the reported total, since
browsers do not send it. Non-identity encoded downloads also report
`total: 0` and `lengthComputable: false`, since `loaded` counts decoded
stream bytes. Cancellation releases the wrapped upload stream.

overloads.signature: type HttpProgressFn = (event: HttpProgressEvent) => Promise<void> | void;

name: HttpRequest
description:
Normalized outgoing HTTP request seen by transports, handlers, interceptors, and `fetchHandler` after the builder runs.

`body` is already the wire value. For JSON that is a **JSON text string**;
sign HMAC or digests against that string (or other final bytes), not the
original struct input.

- `bodyContentType` holds the inferred type of the builder's body. `null` suppresses that header. FormData owns its multipart boundary. HTTP inference follows a direct write to `body` and is not copied by object spread; an explicit `bodyContentType` assignment is copied. A replacement body is detected again, so declare its type with a `content-type` header. For the unchanged body, `null` suppresses library inference when there is no explicit header, but native Fetch may add its own string type.
- HTTP never writes inferred Content-Type into `headers`; interceptors see only declared headers. An explicit `content-type` header always wins over `bodyContentType` and detection, whether set by the builder, client defaults, an interceptor, or a raw `fetchHandler` request. `body: undefined` has no library-inferred Content-Type. Signers should read `headers.get('content-type') ?? request.bodyContentType`; do not configure internal fields.
- `endpoint` is the path with path parameters filled in; `baseEndpoint` is the endpoint selected for this call.
- `query` is the one query the request sends. Interceptors change it in place or pass a replacement to `next()`. A builder that returns `URLSearchParams` has it copied, and a `QuerySerializer` string is parsed into it.
- `meta` is the definition's application-defined metadata (`{ readonly [key: string]: unknown }`): one object, forwarded by reference to every call, attempt, balancer pick, and client. Interceptors read it here and balancers read it as `PickInfo.meta`; both see it read-only. The read-only type is shallow, so nested objects stay shared. Keep per-call state in the interceptor's closure. A replacement passed as `next({ ...request, meta })` reaches only the interceptors after this one, not the balancer or later attempts. Defjs core never reads or copies `meta`, and it is never sent with the request.
- `downloadProgress` and `uploadProgress` are the `onDownloadProgress` and `onUploadProgress` hooks of `HttpExecuteOptions`.
- `responseType` and `errorResponseType` are readonly: they are derived from the endpoint's `output` and `error` struct kinds and must not be changed. Each is set only when its struct is declared. An interceptor that short-circuits with `makeResponse` reads them to match the transport.

typeTable.name: baseEndpoint
typeTable.description: Endpoint selected for this call; its origin and directory bound the resolved path.

typeTable.name: body
typeTable.type: string | number | boolean | object | ArrayBuffer | Blob | FormData | ReadableStream<Uint8Array<ArrayBufferLike>> | URLSearchParams | null | undefined

typeTable.name: bodyContentType
typeTable.description:
Current body media type; null suppresses the header. FormData owns its boundary.
HTTP inference follows direct body mutations and is not copied by object spread; explicit assignments are copied.

typeTable.name: endpoint
typeTable.description: Relative path validated after building and again when an interceptor calls the transport.

typeTable.name: headers
typeTable.description: HTTP interceptors see declared headers; detected Content-Type is applied at the Fetch boundary.

typeTable.name: meta
typeTable.description: Application-defined metadata from the definition, shared by every call. Read-only; never sent with the request.

typeTable.name: query
typeTable.description: The query the request sends. Its wire form is `query.toString()`, the URL Standard's application/x-www-form-urlencoded serialization, so a space is `+`. An empty query adds no `?`.

typeTable.name: responseType
typeTable.description:
Representation for a 2xx body, derived from the endpoint `output` struct kind.
Set only when `output` is declared. Interceptors that short-circuit with `makeResponse`
read this to match the transport. Must not be changed. `undefined` leaves the 2xx body unread.

typeTable.name: errorResponseType
typeTable.description:
Representation for a non-2xx body, derived from the endpoint `error` struct kind.
Set only when `error` is declared. Must not be changed. `undefined` leaves the non-2xx body
unread and does not fall back to `responseType`.

typeTable.name: correlationId
typeTable.description: Per-call identifier shared across all attempts of one HTTP execution, including retries. Read-only; never sent automatically as an HTTP header.

typeTable.name: retryAttempt
typeTable.description: Zero-based retry attempt count for this HTTP execution (`0` on the initial attempt, `1` on the first retry, and so on). Read-only.

typeTable.name: finalizeHeaders
typeTable.description:
Called once per HTTP attempt. The hook receives the outgoing headers after interceptors and before the default `Accept` is filled in, plus the resolved URL.
A throw fails the call with `EXT_HOOK_FAILED`, with the thrown value as `cause`. It is not an endpoint attempt and is not retried.
typeTable.type: ((request: HttpRequest, headers: Headers, url: URL) => void) | undefined

name: HttpRequestShape
description:
Request shape an HTTP builder returns: path, query, headers, and body.

`P` is the endpoint path and `M` its method. `GET` and `HEAD` cannot return a
body. `BodyValue` is a wire value Fetch sends as is (`string`, `Blob`,
`ArrayBuffer`, a typed array or `DataView`, `FormData`, `URLSearchParams`,
`ReadableStream<Uint8Array>`) or JSON data (`number`, `boolean`, `bigint`,
`Date`, `null`, an array, or an object type with string keys); an `interface`
value or class instance needs `{ ...value }`. `path` values must be scalars.
A header value may be a scalar or an array of scalars, and `HeadersInit` is
accepted. `query` may nest, and a nested object needs `withQuerySerializer`
at runtime. `FlatRecord`, `QueryRecord`, `PathValue`, and `BodyValue` are
internal helper types.

typeTable.name: body
typeTable.description:
Request body. Not allowed for GET or HEAD.
Other methods send a native body or encoded JSON, depending on the value.

typeTable.name: headers
typeTable.description:
HeadersInit or a flat record of scalars or scalar arrays.
Put cross-request policies on the Client.

typeTable.name: path
typeTable.description:
Explicit values for path placeholders. Anonymous objects use template keys;
typed objects apply their struct aliases.

typeTable.name: query
typeTable.description:
URLSearchParams passes through unchanged; objects are encoded first.
Configure the Client's query serializer for nested query values.

name: HttpResponse
description:
Wire-shape HTTP response that transports produce and interceptors accept.

`body` is parsed JSON, text, a `Blob`, or an `ArrayBuffer`, according to
`responseType`, not a decoded struct value. `body` is `undefined` when no body
was present; a JSON `null` stays `null`. For a JSON representation, a string
is a JSON string root and is not parsed again; bytes and blobs are raw and
are parsed once. `ok` is true for status codes in the 2xx range. A transport
failure is a fault, never a response. `DecodedResponse` is what reaches the
caller. The symbol key is an internal brand. Build values with `makeResponse`.

typeTable.name: body
typeTable.description: Absent when no body was present. JSON `null` stays `null`.

name: HttpResponseType
description:
Representation used to read an HTTP body before struct validation.

Chosen from the declared struct kind: `string` is `text`, `blob` and `file`
are `blob`, `arrayBuffer` is `arraybuffer` (bytes), and every other kind is
`json`. Not a field on `defineRequest`. It appears on `HttpRequest` as
`responseType` and `errorResponseType`.

overloads.signature: type HttpResponseType = "arraybuffer" | "blob" | "json" | "text";

name: MakeResponseOptions
description:
Fields accepted by `makeResponse` when building a synthetic `HttpResponse`, for example in interceptors.

`status` defaults to `0` and `statusText` to `''`. `url` and `headers` default
to values taken from `request`: its resolved URL (base endpoint, path and
query) and a copy of its headers. A request without `baseEndpoint` gives its
`endpoint` as written. Without a request, `url` is `''` and `headers` is
empty. An omitted `body` stays `undefined`; only an explicit `null` is a JSON
`null`.

name: RequestDefinition
description:
Contract for an HTTP endpoint: method, path, optional input, and the structs that decode its bodies.

Declaring `input` requires an explicit `builder` to place the parsed value on
the request. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides
where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.
`output` declares the body for a 2xx response, `error` the body for anything
else. Only one of the two ever runs, and omitting one means that body is never
read. `ResponseDeclaration` is an internal helper type: `output` and `error`
are required only when the matching type parameter is a struct. The struct
kind selects how a declared body is read. Pass to `defineRequest` to get a
typed endpoint.

name: RequestEndpoint
description:
Operation returned by `defineRequest`.

The first argument is a {@link Client}. Further arguments are the input, and only the input: none when the definition declares no `input`, optional when the input struct accepts `undefined`, and required otherwise. Calling it starts the request and returns the error-first tuple.

overloads.signature:
type RequestEndpoint<
  Args extends unknown[],
  Data,
  ErrorData,
  Response extends HttpMeta,
> = (
  client: Client,
  ...args: Args
) => Promise<
  | [err: null, result: Data, response: Response]
  | [err: FaultOf<ErrorData>, result: undefined, response: undefined]
>;

name: RequestErrorData
description: Decoded error body for the declared `error` struct, or `undefined` when none is declared.

overloads.signature:
type RequestErrorData<TError extends AnyStruct | undefined> =
  DeclaredBody<TError>;

name: RequestSuccessData
description: Decoded success body for the declared `output` struct, or `undefined` when none is declared.

overloads.signature:
type RequestSuccessData<TOutput extends AnyStruct | undefined> =
  DeclaredBody<TOutput>;

name: UseRequestConfig
description:
HTTP fields of {@link RequestOptions}: progress callbacks, `retry`, and `signal`.

`onDownloadProgress` and `onUploadProgress` are {@link HttpProgressFn}
callbacks. They receive an {@link HttpProgressEvent} with `loaded`, `total`,
and `lengthComputable`. `retry` replaces the client's retry policy for this
call. Other request fields are ignored by HTTP.

typeTable.name: signal
typeTable.description: Aborts the call.

typeTable.name: onDownloadProgress
typeTable.description: Observes download progress.

typeTable.name: onUploadProgress
typeTable.description: Observes upload progress.

typeTable.name: retry
typeTable.description: Retry policy for this call. Replaces the client policy as a whole value; the `budget` stays with the client.

name: createResolvedRequestUrl
description:
Resolves a relative definition path under the base endpoint's origin and directory into a URL.

During an operation, a missing, relative, or invalid base or an illegal
path becomes `REQ_BUILD_FAILED` before any interceptor or transport runs,
including a short-circuiting interceptor, for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket alike.
An interceptor's final `req.endpoint` is also validated against its final
`req.baseEndpoint`; deliberately replacing the base with another valid
absolute URL is allowed. Deterministic URL errors are never retried.
throws: TypeError when the endpoint or path is invalid.

parameters.name: baseEndpoint
parameters.description: A valid absolute client endpoint. Its query and hash are dropped, and a trailing slash is added to its pathname so that the base path is kept: `https://api.example.com/v1` with `/users` gives `https://api.example.com/v1/users`.

parameters.name: path
parameters.description: A relative endpoint path. A single leading slash is removed. After resolution, the URL must keep the base origin and stay under its directory. Absolute or protocol-relative paths, C0 control characters (including tab, CR, and LF), backslashes, `?`, `#`, and directory escapes are rejected. Scheme-like and protocol-relative forms are rejected even with leading spaces; a plain inner space is allowed and sent as `%20`.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: The URL's search without a leading `?`, as `URLSearchParams.toString()` gives it. When non-empty it is set as the URL's `search`.

name: defineRequest
description:
Declares a typed HTTP request endpoint.

Pass method, path, an optional input struct, and the single `output` and
`error` structs. Call the returned operation with a client and, when declared, the input.

The contract is `method`, `path`, an optional `input` struct, optional
`output` and `error` structs, and an optional `meta`. A declared `input`
always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters;
the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without
`input` may omit `builder`. `ResponseDeclaration` and `BuilderField` are
internal helper types: `output` and `error` are required only when the
matching type parameter is a struct, and `builder` is
`(input: BuilderInput<TInput>) => HttpRequestShape` when `input` is declared.

`output` is one struct for the 2xx body; `error` is one struct for every
non-2xx body. Neither is keyed by status. A declaration is an assertion:
omitting one means that body is never read.

Known fields are copied when the definition is created. `builder`, `input`, `output`, `error`, and `meta` keep their identity. A getter on one of those fields runs during `defineRequest` and its exception escapes the call. Other properties on the definition object are not read.
returns:
An operation `(client, ...input) => Promise<error-first tuple>`.

The checked example file passes the whole input object as `path`. This snippet maps individual fields into `path` and `query` instead:

tags.name: example
tags.text:
```ts
const getOrder = defineRequest({
  method: 'GET',
  path: '/orders/:id',
  input: struct.object({ id: struct.number(), verbose: struct.boolean() }),
  builder: (input) => ({ path: { id: input.id }, query: { verbose: input.verbose } }),
  output: struct.object({ id: struct.number(), status: struct.string() }),
})
```

parameters.name: definition
parameters.description: Request contract (method, path, input, builder, output, error, meta).

name: fetchHandler
description:
Default HTTP transport: perform `httpRequest` with `fetch` and return an `HttpResponse`.

The client always uses it; `withHTTPHandle` only supplies the `fetchImpl` it
calls. Also usable in tests and custom handlers. `fetchImpl` defaults to the
global `fetch` resolved at send time. It rejects, rather than resolving with
a synthetic response, when no response reached the client.
returns:
Parsed `HttpResponse`. Rejects when no response reached the client, when reading the body
failed, when an upload observer threw (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`), or when `finalizeHeaders` threw (`EXT_HOOK_FAILED`).
A request that is invalid before it is sent rejects with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`: a method that is not a token or is
forbidden, a GET or HEAD body, a URL with credentials, a `bodyContentType` the platform refuses as a header value,
or, when `uploadProgress` is set, a stream body that is already locked or read. Cancellation still wins.
The `body` of a `HEAD` response, or of a `204`, `205`, or `304` response, is absent whether or not the engine exposes a body stream.

parameters.name: httpRequest
parameters.description: Normalized request (URL, headers, body, signal, progress hooks).

parameters.name: fetchImpl
parameters.description:
Fetch implementation; defaults to global `fetch`. The library default handle is called as
`(url, init)` while the global is untouched, and its body is read in one piece unless download progress is observed. Any other handle receives a
`Request` and its body is read chunk by chunk.

name: makeResponse
description:
Builds an `HttpResponse` without a network call, for interceptors that short-circuit `next` and for tests.

Default status is `0`, so pass a 2xx `status` for a success. `ok` is true for
2xx. The value it returns goes through the same media-type check and the same
declared struct as one off the wire; there is no trusted short-circuit. For a
JSON body, set a JSON `content-type` header.
returns: An `HttpResponse` with `ok` derived from the status code.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Status, headers, body, and an optional request to copy headers/url from; defaults yield status `0`.

name: EventStreamCloseInfo
description:
How an SSE stream ended: clean EOF, abort, or an error carrying its fault `code`.

The discriminant is `kind` so that `code` can mean the same thing it means on a fault.

The value of `EventStreamHandle.closed`. `eof` means the response ended normally. `aborted` means the stream was closed with `close()` or disposal, or its caller signal aborted with a non-timeout reason; `reason` and `cause` carry the value passed to `close`. `close()`, disposal and a caller signal abort all discard the events nobody has read yet, as `EventSource.close()` does, whether or not the stream had already ended (the response ended, or it failed), and the iterator ends at once. A stop after the stream ended discards the unread events and changes nothing else: `closed` keeps its value, and an iterator that rejects with the `cause` of an `error` end still rejects with it once no unread event is left. If the caller signal aborts after open and before the stream has ended with a `TimeoutError` or `ERR_TIMEOUT`, the iterator throws `ERR_TIMEOUT` and `closed` is `{ kind: 'error', code: 'NET_TIMEOUT', ... }`; a deadline that expires after the stream has ended is a stop and discards the unread events. Explicit `close(timeoutError)` still reports `aborted`. `error` carries the fault `code` (see `EventStreamFaultCode`) and the failure as `cause`. A reconnect pick that fails after open, or that gives a URL the request cannot use (invalid, or with credentials), uses `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`. A reconnect handshake that ends the stream with a non-2xx status uses `HTTP_STATUS`, and its `cause` is the `HTTP_STATUS` fault, as for a failed first handshake. `closed` resolves when the connection ends, which can be before the iterator has read every event. After an `error` end, including a timeout, the events already queued are still delivered and the iterator rejects after the last one, unless the caller stops the stream first.

overloads.signature:
type EventStreamCloseInfo =
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "eof" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { kind: "aborted" })
  | (EventStreamCloseInfoBase & { code: EventStreamFaultCode; kind: "error" });

name: EventStreamData
description:
Union of parsed SSE events inferred from an EventStructs map.

For each declared event name except `default`, the union has `{ event: <name>; data: Infer<TEvents[name]>; id?: string }`. When a `default` struct is declared, it adds `{ event: string; data: Infer<TEvents['default']>; id?: string }` for every event name that has no struct of its own. `KnownEventUnion` and `DefaultEventUnion` are internal helper types.

overloads.signature:
type EventStreamData<TEvents extends EventStructs> =
  TEvents extends EventStructs
    ? KnownEventUnion<TEvents> | DefaultEventUnion<TEvents>
    : never;

name: EventStreamDefinition
description:
Contract that describes an SSE endpoint for defineEventStream.

The composed members are:

- `path` and `events`, plus optional `method` (default `'GET'`), `meta`, and `maxBufferSize` (default `64 * 1024` bytes). A frame larger than `maxBufferSize` ends the stream with `CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED`. The library holds at most 1024 events waiting for the `for await` consumer; when they are full, reading the response pauses until the consumer takes one. No event is dropped for lack of room and the stream does not fail.

- `error`, required only when `TError` is a struct. It decodes the body of a failed handshake (a non-2xx response). The kind rule is the same as for HTTP: `string` is text, `blob` and `file` are blobs, `arrayBuffer` is bytes, and everything else is JSON.

- `input` and `builder`. The request shape matches HTTP, including `body`; `GET` and `HEAD` cannot return a body. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.

`EventStreamDefinitionBase` and `EventStreamErrorField` are internal helper types.

name: EventStreamEndpoint
description:
Operation returned by `defineEventStream`.

The first argument is a {@link Client}. Further arguments are the input only. Calling it opens the stream and returns the existing error-first tuple.

overloads.signature:
type EventStreamEndpoint<
  Args extends unknown[],
  Event,
  TError extends AnyStruct | undefined = undefined,
> = (
  client: Client,
  ...args: Args
) => Promise<StreamAwaitResult<Event, TError>>;

name: EventStreamExecuteOptions
description:
SSE fields of {@link RequestOptions}. HTTP progress and WebSocket fields are ignored.

`signal` covers the whole stream, including after it opens. For a deadline on the connection handshake alone, pass `retry: { maxRetries: 0, attemptTimeoutMs }`. `retry` replaces the client's retry policy for this call.

typeTable.name: signal
typeTable.description: Aborts the stream, including after it is open.

typeTable.name: retry
typeTable.description: Retry policy for this call. Replaces the client policy as a whole value; the `budget` is HTTP only.

name: EventStreamFaultCode
description:
Fault codes an event stream can end with, drawn from the one shared `FaultCode` namespace.

A subset of the shared `FaultCode` set. It is the `code` of an `EventStreamCloseInfo` with `kind: 'error'`.
`REQ_BUILD_FAILED` means a reconnect pick failed after the stream opened, or the picked endpoint gave an invalid URL or a URL with credentials. It stays that code; it is not rewritten to `NET_UNREACHABLE`.
`HTTP_STATUS` means a reconnect handshake answered with a non-2xx status; `cause` is then the same `HTTP_STATUS` fault a failed first handshake returns.

overloads.signature:
type EventStreamFaultCode = Extract<
  FaultCode,
  | "CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED"
  | "EXT_HOOK_FAILED"
  | "EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED"
  | "HTTP_STATUS"
  | "NET_TIMEOUT"
  | "NET_UNREACHABLE"
  | "REQ_BUILD_FAILED"
  | "RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID"
>;

name: EventStreamHandle
EventStreamOpenInfo
description:
Metadata available once an SSE response has opened.

`response` is the handshake response and `url` is the resolved request URL. It is the third element of a successful event-stream result and the value of `EventStreamHandle.open`.

name: EventStreamRequestShape
description: Request shape an SSE builder returns: the same fields as {@link HttpRequestShape} for method `M` and path `P`.

overloads.signature:
type EventStreamRequestShape<
  P extends string,
  M extends string,
> = HttpRequestShape<P, M>;

name: EventStructs
description:
Map from SSE event names to the structs that decode their data.

An event with no `event:` field is named `message`. An event whose name has no own entry uses the `default` struct; with neither, the event is skipped and `onInvalidEvent` is called. Declare the event name `__proto__` with a computed own key.

A `string` event struct keeps the raw `data` text. Every other kind is JSON text: `JSON.parse`, then the struct. A bare `struct.literal` therefore needs JSON text, not an unquoted token.

Retries live on the client (`withRetry`).

overloads.signature: type EventStructs = { [key: string]: AnyStruct };

name: StreamAwaitResult
description:
Await-result tuple from opening an SSE stream.

- On success: `[null, stream, open]`. `open` is the returned connection's first successful handshake snapshot for native Defjs handles or wrappers forwarding the same live `open` object; custom handles or wrappers overriding `open` use their current public `open` even after reconnect, while `stream.open` stays live.

- On failure: `[err, undefined, open]`. `open` carries the response snapshot when the failure happened after a response arrived, for example a non-2xx handshake, and is `undefined` otherwise.

- `TError` is the declared `error` struct. It types the decoded error body on the fault.

- A non-2xx handshake is an `HTTP_STATUS` fault whose `data` is the decoded `error` body. When the declared `error` body could not be decoded, startup returns the decode fault instead, as `defineRequest` does: `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID` for a JSON declaration that meets another media type, `RES_DECODE_FAILED` for an unreadable or unparsable body, `RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH` for a body that does not match the struct. Its `status` and `response` carry the handshake status as metadata and `cause` holds the reason. Interceptors, `shouldRetry` and a reconnect's `closed` still receive `HTTP_STATUS`, with the same `cause`, so a gateway `503` is retried however its body looks.

- A 2xx handshake whose media type is not `text/event-stream` is `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID`. One with that media type and no body (a `204` or `205` on Node.js and Bun) is an empty stream: the call succeeds and `closed` settles `{ kind: 'eof' }` at once.

overloads.signature:
type StreamAwaitResult<
  TEvent,
  TError extends AnyStruct | undefined = undefined,
> =
  | [err: null, stream: EventStreamHandle<TEvent>, open: EventStreamOpenInfo]
  | [
      err: Fault<TError> | HttpStatusFaultOf<undefined>,
      stream: undefined,
      open: EventStreamOpenInfo | undefined,
    ];

name: defineEventStream
description:
Declare a typed Server-Sent Events endpoint.

Pass path and event structs. Call the returned operation
with a client and, when declared, the input.

- **definition** — `path` and an `events` map. Optional `method` (default `'GET'`), `meta`, `input`, `error`, and `maxBufferSize` (default `64 * 1024` bytes). A frame larger than `maxBufferSize` ends the stream with `CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED`; the library holds at most 1024 unread events, and a full queue pauses reading the response until the consumer takes an event. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.

`EventStreamDefinitionBase`, `EventStreamErrorField`, and `BuilderField` are internal helper types: `error` is required only when `TError` is a struct, and `builder` is `(input: BuilderInput<TInput>) => EventStreamRequestShape` when `input` is declared.

Known fields are copied when the definition is created. The `events` dictionary container is copied, including own non-enumerable keys, and inherited names are left behind. Struct values, `builder`, `input`, `error`, and `meta` keep their identity. An accessor on that dictionary still runs when a message arrives, with the original dictionary as `this`. A getter on a fixed definition field runs during `defineEventStream`.

parameters.name: definition
parameters.description: SSE contract (path, events, optional input and limits).

name: ManualSocketCloseReason
description:
Close code and reason recorded when a session is closed with session.close.

Records the `code` and `reason` passed to `session.close(code?, reason?)`. They fill `code` and `reason` of the final `{ kind: 'closed' }` close info when the peer's close event carries none. `close` throws a `DOMException` when a provided `code` is not the integer `1000` or an integer from `3000` through `4999`, and when `reason` exceeds 123 UTF-8 bytes. Omitting `code` is allowed.

name: SocketAwaitResult
description:
Await-result tuple from opening a WebSocket.

- On success: `[null, session, connection]`. `session.connection` moves forward on reconnect. The tuple's `connection` preserves the first successful snapshot only for a native Defjs session or a wrapper forwarding the same live `connection` object. Custom sessions and wrappers that transform `connection` instead return their current public `connection`. Sharing `closed` cannot bypass URL sanitization or metadata filtering, and Defjs does not reconstruct first-connection metadata from arbitrary transformations.

- On failure: `[err, undefined, connection]`. `connection` may be `undefined`, for example when the constructor failed before the socket opened.

- Only startup failures arrive here. Once the session is returned, later errors surface through `onRuntimeError`, `receive`, and `closed`.

overloads.signature:
type SocketAwaitResult<TIncoming, TOutgoing = never> =
  | [
      err: null,
      session: WebSocketSession<TIncoming, TOutgoing>,
      connection: WebSocketConnectionInfo,
    ]
  | [
      err: Fault<undefined>,
      session: undefined,
      connection: WebSocketConnectionInfo | undefined,
    ];

name: SocketLifecycleOutcome
description:
The outcome of a **single connect attempt**, not the final result of the session.

The retry logic uses it to decide whether to try again.

- `closeInfo` holds the close details of that attempt: `{ code?, reason?, wasClean? }`.

- `connection` is the connection snapshot, when the attempt got one.

- `cause` is the error that ended the attempt, if any.

- `opened` tells whether the socket reached `open` before it ended.

`shouldRetry` does not receive this object. Its context carries `attempt`, `cause`, `code`, `reason`, and `wasClean`, taken from it. The final result of the session is {@link WebSocketCloseInfo}.

name: UseWebSocketConfig
description:
WebSocket fields of {@link RequestOptions}, plus `signal`.

`beforeConnect`, `heartbeat`, `protocols`, and `retry` override the client-level options for one call. `signal` covers the whole session, including after it opens. For a deadline on connecting alone, pass `retry: { maxRetries: 0, attemptTimeoutMs }`. There is no `abort` field.

typeTable.type: ((context: { attempt: number; signal: AbortSignal; }) => void | Promise<void>) | undefined

typeTable.name: signal
typeTable.description: Aborts the session, including after it is open.

name: WebSocketCloseInfo
description:
Logical terminal outcome of a WebSocket session.

What `session.closed` resolves with, once the session has ended for good.

- `closed`: the session ended normally. When the peer or the server closed it, the messages already queued are still delivered through `receive` before it ends, unless the caller stops the session first. A manual `session.close()` or disposal is a stop by the caller: the messages nobody has read yet are discarded and `receive` ends at once.

- `aborted`: the session was cancelled; `cause` is the abort reason. Messages nobody has read yet are discarded.

- `error`: the session failed; `cause` is required. The error is passed to `onRuntimeError`. Runtime causes need not carry a Defjs fault code; heartbeat timeout and exhausted reconnects can retain plain errors. A connection that was open and then dropped without a close frame (`code` 1006) is an `error` on every runtime, with `cause` `Error("WebSocket connection error")`; the runtime need not fire a native `error` event for it. Messages already queued are still delivered through `receive`, unless the caller stops the session first; it rejects with `cause` after the last one.

- `code`, `reason`, and `wasClean` come from the native close event when one was observed. A manual `session.close(code, reason)` fills `code` and `reason` when the close event does not.

A stop by the caller (`session.close()`, disposal, or an abort of the caller's `signal`) discards the messages nobody has read yet, whether or not the session had already ended (the peer closed it, or it failed). A stop after the session ended discards the unread messages and changes nothing else: `closed` keeps its value, and `receive` still rejects with the `cause` of an `error` end once no unread message is left. A `signal` that expires with a `TimeoutError` while the session is still running is a timeout, not a stop: the session ends as an `error` and delivers the queued messages first. A deadline that expires after the session has ended is a stop.

name: WebSocketConnectionInfo
description:
Connection metadata for the current WebSocket generation.

- `url` is the URL the socket reports.

- `protocol` is the negotiated subprotocol and `extensions` the negotiated extensions. Both are `undefined` when the socket reports an empty string.

- `generation` counts the physical sockets that reached `open`: `1` after the first open, one more after each reconnect. A snapshot taken before any open has `0`.

`session.connection` exposes the session's current public connection info. The `connection` in the operation result preserves the first successful snapshot only for a native Defjs session or a wrapper forwarding the same live `connection` object. Custom sessions and wrappers that transform `connection` instead return their current public `connection`. Sharing `closed` cannot bypass URL sanitization or metadata filtering, and Defjs does not reconstruct first-connection metadata from arbitrary transformations.

name: WebSocketDefinition
description:
Contract object passed to defineWebSocket.

- `incoming` is the struct every received frame is parsed with. Frames are JSON text.

- `outgoing` is the struct `session.send` validates and encodes with. Without it, `send` throws.

- `maxOutgoingQueueSize` is how many messages are kept while the session is `reconnecting`; it defaults to `0`, which disables queueing of messages sent in that state. Incoming messages are not bounded by a count: the library queues every message the platform delivers until `receive` reads it.

- `protocols` is the static default subprotocol list. `RequestOptions.protocols` and {@link withWebSocketProtocols} override it.

- `meta` is application-defined metadata (`{ [key: string]: unknown }`) that flows through interceptors and balancers, read-only there and shared by every connection of this definition. Defjs core never reads it, and it is never sent with the request.

- `input` is the struct for the operation input. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`. The builder may return `path` and `query` only; see {@link WebSocketRequestShape}.

name: WebSocketEndpoint
description:
Operation returned by `defineWebSocket`.

The first argument is a {@link Client}. Further arguments are the input only. Calling it opens the session and returns the existing error-first tuple.

overloads.signature:
type WebSocketEndpoint<
  Args extends unknown[],
  Incoming,
  Outgoing = never,
> = (
  client: Client,
  ...args: Args
) => Promise<SocketAwaitResult<Incoming, Outgoing>>;

name: WebSocketExecuteOptions
description:
WebSocket fields read from {@link RequestOptions} for one call.

See {@link UseWebSocketConfig}. `heartbeat` callbacks are not inferred from the operation; narrow `unknown` messages yourself.

overloads.signature:
type WebSocketExecuteOptions<
  TIncoming = unknown,
  TOutgoing = unknown,
> = UseWebSocketConfig<TIncoming, TOutgoing>;

name: WebSocketHeartbeatConfig
description:
Heartbeat settings for a live WebSocket session: what to send, how often, and how to recognize the answer.

Defjs defines no heartbeat format. `message` and `isAck` are yours.

- `intervalMs` is the delay between heartbeat messages.

- `message()` builds the payload. It is sent through the `outgoing` struct as JSON text, so the endpoint needs an `outgoing` struct. Nothing is sent when it returns `undefined`.

- After struct encoding, non-JSON values fail with `TypeError` through the same serializer as `session.send`; that heartbeat failure ends the session without a retry.

- `isAck(message)` receives each decoded incoming message. When it returns `true`, the message is the acknowledgement and is not delivered to `receive`. A frame that fails the `incoming` struct never reaches it.

- `timeoutMs` is how long to wait for an acknowledgement after a heartbeat, and it needs `isAck`: the type allows `timeoutMs` only together with `isAck`. A missing acknowledgement counts as a connection failure, reported to the balancer as `NET_UNREACHABLE`. The socket is closed and the attempt enters the retry flow of `withRetry`; without a retry policy the session ends with an `error`. A throwing `message()` or a serialization failure also ends the session, but is not attributed to the endpoint and is not retried.

Set it with {@link withWebSocketHeartbeat} or the `heartbeat` request option.

name: WebSocketIncomingData
description:
Decoded type of a received WebSocket message.

The type of each message yielded by `session.receive`: the {@link Infer} output of the endpoint's `incoming` struct. Aliased fields use their logical names.

overloads.signature:
type WebSocketIncomingData<TIncoming extends AnyStruct> =
  Infer<TIncoming>;

name: WebSocketOutgoingData
description:
Type accepted by WebSocket session send.

The type `session.send` accepts: the {@link StructInput} of the endpoint's `outgoing` struct, or `never` when the endpoint declares none, so `send` cannot be called with a value.

overloads.signature:
type WebSocketOutgoingData<TOutgoing extends AnyStruct | undefined> =
  TOutgoing extends AnyStruct ? StructInput<TOutgoing> : never;

name: WebSocketRequestShape
description:
Request shape the `builder` of a {@link WebSocketDefinition} may return, where `P` is the endpoint path.

- `path` supplies the `:name` segments of `P`: one scalar value per name. It is `never` when the path has none.
- `query` is a `URLSearchParams` or a record of scalars, arrays, and nested records.
- `headers` and `body` are `never`. A WebSocket handshake takes neither from the builder; put credentials in `beforeConnect` or an interceptor.

typeTable.description: WebSocket handshakes cannot have a body. Use session.send after connecting.

Explicit values for path placeholders. Anonymous objects use template keys;

name: WebSocketSession
description:
Typed WebSocket session: send and receive messages, observe state, and close.

- `state` is the logical {@link WebSocketState}; `connection` is the latest {@link WebSocketConnectionInfo}. `bufferedAmount` is the native unsent byte count, or `0` with no physical socket.

- `receive` yields incoming messages already parsed with the `incoming` struct. It is one-consumer: asking for a second iterator throws a `TypeError`. A frame that cannot be parsed is reported to `onRuntimeError` listeners and skipped. When the transport fails (for example a drop without a close frame), messages already received are delivered first, then `receive` rejects with `closed.cause`. Cancellation by the caller (`signal` abort), `close()` and disposal discard the messages nobody has read yet, whether or not the session had already ended; a heartbeat timeout or a transport failure ends with an error after the queued messages are delivered, and a stop after that error discards the unread messages while `receive` still rejects with `closed.cause`. A `signal` that expires with a timeout while the session is open is not a stop, but one that expires after the session ended is.

- `send(message)` validates and encodes the message with the `outgoing` struct, then sends JSON text. It sends immediately while `open`, queues while `reconnecting` when `maxOutgoingQueueSize` allows, and throws a `DOMException` named `InvalidStateError` when the session is not writable. It also throws when no `outgoing` struct is declared, the message fails the struct, or the queue is disabled or full.

- After encoding, a value JSON cannot faithfully represent throws `TypeError` before sending or entering the queue. This includes non-finite numbers, functions, symbols, `Map`, `Set`, streams, and class instances without a JSON representation, at the root or nested. The same guard protects heartbeat messages; a heartbeat serialization failure ends the session. Struct validation may reject a value first.

- `close(code?, reason?)` requests closure and stops the heartbeat. `code` must be `1000` or in `3000..4999`, and `reason` at most 123 UTF-8 bytes; invalid arguments throw before the state changes.

- `closed` resolves with the logical terminal {@link WebSocketCloseInfo}.

- `onStateChange` and `onRuntimeError` return an unsubscribe function.

Prefer `await using ownedSession = session` for owned scope cleanup. Manual `session.close()` and `await session.closed` remain available.

```ts
async function consume(
  session: WebSocketSession<unknown, never>,
): Promise<void> {
  await using ownedSession = session;
  for await (const message of ownedSession.receive) console.log(message);
}
```

The async disposer requests native close and waits for Defjs-owned teardown, but it bounds a missing close event at one second and may reject with a `DOMException` named `TimeoutError`. It cannot prove that the physical TCP connection closed.

name: WebSocketState
description:
Lifecycle state of a managed WebSocket session.

| State          | Meaning                                                                |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `idle`         | Before the first connect attempt                                       |
| `connecting`   | Preparing and opening the first connection                             |
| `open`         | The physical socket is open                                            |
| `reconnecting` | Preparing or waiting for a replacement socket after a close            |
| `closing`      | Closure was requested with `session.close()` or disposal               |
| `closed`       | Terminal: the session ended without an error or cancellation           |
| `aborted`      | Terminal: the session was cancelled through `signal`                   |
| `error`        | Terminal: the session failed, including a startup failure or `timeout` |

Observe it with `session.state` and `session.onStateChange`.

overloads.signature:
type WebSocketState =
  | "aborted"
  | "closed"
  | "closing"
  | "connecting"
  | "error"
  | "idle"
  | "open"
  | "reconnecting";

name: defineWebSocket
description:
Declare a typed WebSocket endpoint.

Pass path and incoming (and optional outgoing) message structs.
Call the returned operation with a client and, when declared, the input.

- **definition** — `path`, one `incoming` struct, and optional `outgoing` and `input` structs, static `protocols`, `maxOutgoingQueueSize`, and `meta`. A declared `input` always requires an explicit `builder`. `input` only defines the parameters; the builder alone decides where each value goes. Only definitions without `input` may omit `builder`.

A WebSocket `builder` may return `path` and `query` only; `headers` and `body` are rejected. `WebSocketDefinitionBase` and `BuilderField` are internal helper types.

Known fields are copied when the definition is created. Structs, `builder`, and `meta` keep their identity. A `protocols` array is copied, so a later edit of the original array does not retarget the endpoint. A getter on a fixed field runs during `defineWebSocket`.

parameters.description: WebSocket contract (path, structs, queue limits, optional input).

name: AnyFault
description:
Any fault at all, whatever its decoded error-body type.

Use it for handlers that classify faults without caring which endpoint produced
them. Prefer `Fault<typeof yourErrorStruct>` where the body type matters.

overloads.signature:
type AnyFault =
  | DecodeFault
  | HttpStatusFaultOf<undefined>
  | HttpStatusFaultOf<unknown>
  | PreflightFault;

name: DecodeFault
description:
A response arrived but could not be read as declared.

`code` is one of `RES_DECODE_FAILED`, `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID`, or
`RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH`. `response` is metadata only: a body is a decoded value,
and decoding is what failed, so there is no `body` field to reach for. The
offending detail lives on `cause` (a `StructError` for a struct mismatch, the
parser failure for an unreadable representation).

name: DecodeFaultCode
description:
Codes whose fault carries response metadata but no body.

These are the `code` values of `DecodeFault`. `PreflightFaultCode` is every
other `FaultCode` except `HTTP_STATUS`.

overloads.signature:
type DecodeFaultCode =
  "RES_DECODE_FAILED" | "RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID" | "RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH";

name: ERR_ABORTED
description:
Shared Error sentinel that marks a request as aborted.

Its `message` is `Request was aborted`. Shared `cause` and message value for caller cancellation. `createNetworkFault`
maps it, and a `DOMException` named `AbortError`, to `NET_ABORTED`. An HTTP
interceptor that throws it makes the call resolve with a `NET_ABORTED` fault.
SSE and WebSocket interceptors that throw it are reported as
`EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED`.

The sentinel carries a non-enumerable `Symbol.for('defjs.cause.aborted')`
brand. {@link isAbortCause} recognizes this sentinel from any Core copy
without comparing object identity. Classification is independent of unrelated
earlier executions.

overloads.signature: const ERR_ABORTED: Error;

name: ERR_TIMEOUT
description:
Shared Error sentinel that marks a request as timed out.

Its `message` is `Request timed out`. Shared `cause` and message value for timeouts. `createNetworkFault` maps it,
and any error named `TimeoutError`, to `NET_TIMEOUT`. An HTTP interceptor
that throws it makes the call resolve with a `NET_TIMEOUT` fault. SSE and
WebSocket interceptors that throw it are reported as `EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED`.

The sentinel carries a non-enumerable `Symbol.for('defjs.cause.timeout')`
brand. {@link isTimeoutCause} recognizes this sentinel from any Core copy
without comparing object identity. Classification is independent of unrelated
earlier executions.

overloads.signature: const ERR_TIMEOUT: Error;

name: Fault
description:
Union of every failure an operation can return, discriminated by `code`.

`Fault<TErr>` is {@link FaultOf} applied to the decoded body type, so it is the
union of {@link DecodeFault}, {@link HttpStatusFault}<TErr>, and
{@link PreflightFault}. `ErrorBody<TErr>` is `undefined` when `TErr` is
`undefined`, and `Infer<TErr>` otherwise. Switch on `fault.code`.

Every variant is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault`, so `String(fault)` produces
`DefjsFault: <message>`. `code` and the variant metadata — `status`, `response`,
`data` — are enumerable own properties. The native `cause` chain is non-enumerable.

Default Struct messages say `received <kind>`, never the received value. A JSON
`SyntaxError` behind `RES_DECODE_FAILED` gives the message
`Response body could not be decoded`. Structural paths retain record keys, which
may be sensitive. Raw `StructIssue.received` and parser causes remain sensitive;
custom `errorMap` and extension messages are used verbatim and need review before
logging.

Call `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` only after narrowing `fault.cause`
to `StructError`; those helpers are not copied onto the fault.
