tags.text: TErr - The endpoint's declared `error` struct, or `undefined` when it declares none.

name: FaultClass
description:
Extracts the class prefix from a fault code: the segment before its first `_`.

`FaultClass<FaultCode>` is
`'CAP' | 'ENV' | 'EXT' | 'HTTP' | 'NET' | 'REQ' | 'RES'`.

tags.name: typeParam
tags.text: C - A `FaultCode`, or a union of them.

name: FaultCode
description:
Every failure Defjs reports, as one closed set of codes.

The prefix before the first `_` is the class; there is no separate `kind` field.
Read the prefix for coarse triage and the whole code for an exact case:

| Class  | Meaning                                                        |
| ------ | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `HTTP` | The peer answered with a non-2xx status.                        |
| `REQ`  | The request never left: input, request options, or build.       |
| `NET`  | No usable response: cancel, timeout, connect, truncated body.   |
| `RES`  | A response arrived but could not be read as declared.           |
| `EXT`  | Code you attached to the pipeline threw.                        |
| `CAP`  | A declared buffer limit was exceeded.                           |
| `ENV`  | The host runtime lacks a required capability.                   |

The set is closed on purpose: it keeps `switch (fault.code)` exhaustive. Extensions
report their own detail through `cause`, not through a new code.

overloads.signature:
type FaultCode =
  | "CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED"
  | "ENV_UNSUPPORTED"
  | "EXT_HOOK_FAILED"
  | "EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED"
  | "EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED"
  | "HTTP_STATUS"
  | "NET_ABORTED"
  | "NET_BODY_INCOMPLETE"
  | "NET_TIMEOUT"
  | "NET_UNREACHABLE"
  | "REQ_BUILD_FAILED"
  | "REQ_INPUT_INVALID"
  | "RES_DECODE_FAILED"
  | "RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID"
  | "RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH";

name: FaultOf
description:
Any failure returned by an operation, expressed by its decoded error-body type.

`Fault<TErr>` is `FaultOf` applied to `Infer<TErr>`, and `HttpAwaitResult` uses
`FaultOf<TErrorData>`. Pass a decoded type, not a struct: write
`FaultOf<Infer<typeof errorStruct>>`, or use `Fault<typeof errorStruct>`.

tags.name: typeParam
tags.text: TData - The decoded `error` body, or `undefined` when no error struct was declared.

overloads.signature:
type FaultOf<TData = undefined> =
  DecodeFault | HttpStatusFaultOf<TData> | PreflightFault;

name: HttpStatusFault
description:
Fault for a non-2xx response, typed by the declared `error` struct.

`TErr` is the endpoint's declared `error` struct, or `undefined` when it
declares none. Any non-2xx status. When the endpoint declared `error` and the
body decoded, `data` is that body and `response` carries it. Omitting `error`
skips decoding, which leaves `data` as `undefined` and `response` without a
`body` field. `ErrorBody<TErr>` is that decoded body: `undefined` when no
error struct was declared, otherwise `Infer<TErr>`. {@link HttpStatusFaultOf}
is the member shape.

overloads.signature:
type HttpStatusFault<TErr extends AnyStruct | undefined = undefined> =
  HttpStatusFaultOf<ErrorBody<TErr>>;

name: HttpStatusFaultOf
description:
Non-2xx fault expressed by its decoded body type instead of the struct that produced it.

Factories work in decoded values, so they use this form; endpoint types use
`HttpStatusFault` and let `Infer` bridge the two. When `TData` is `undefined`,
the body was never read and `response` is metadata alone.

name: PreflightFault
description:
A failure that may have happened before any response existed.

Covers `REQ_*`, `NET_*`, `EXT_*`, `CAP_*`, and `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`. `response`
is `undefined` until the transport has metadata to report, such as a
body that truncated mid-download.

name: PreflightFaultCode
description:
Codes whose fault may never have reached a response.

Every `FaultCode` except `HTTP_STATUS` and the decode codes:
`CAP_BUFFER_EXCEEDED`, `ENV_UNSUPPORTED`, `EXT_HOOK_FAILED`,
`EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED`, `EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`, `NET_ABORTED`, `NET_BODY_INCOMPLETE`, `NET_TIMEOUT`, `NET_UNREACHABLE`,
`REQ_BUILD_FAILED`, and `REQ_INPUT_INVALID`. These
are the `code` values of `PreflightFault`.

overloads.signature:
type PreflightFaultCode = Exclude<
  FaultCode,
  DecodeFaultCode | "HTTP_STATUS"
>;

name: createDecodeFault
description:
Builds a decode fault for a response that arrived but could not be read as declared.

`code` is `RES_DECODE_FAILED`, `RES_MEDIA_TYPE_INVALID`, or
`RES_STRUCT_MISMATCH`. The fault carries metadata only: a body is a decoded
value, and decoding is what failed, so there is no `body`. `status` is copied
from `response`. The result is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault`.

`cause` is the underlying parser or struct failure and is kept as `cause`.
Its message normally becomes the fault message (`String(cause)` when it is
not an `Error`). For `RES_DECODE_FAILED` with an `Error` named `SyntaxError`,
the message is `Response body could not be decoded`, so `String(fault)` does
not include a body fragment. Default Struct messages contain received kinds,
not values; raw values and parser text remain on the cause.
returns: A decode fault with no body.

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: Which read step failed.

parameters.name: cause
parameters.description: Underlying parser or struct failure.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: Metadata of the response that could not be read.

name: createHttpStatusFault
description:
Builds an `HTTP_STATUS` fault for a non-2xx response whose body decoded against the declared `error` struct.

The fault is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault` with `code: 'HTTP_STATUS'`,
`data` set to `response.body`, `status` copied from the response, and
`response` as passed. The message is `Http failure response: <status>`,
followed by ` - <statusText>` when there is one.

Use {@link createUndecodedHttpStatusFault} when no body was decoded.
returns: An `HTTP_STATUS` fault whose `data` is that body.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: The response, carrying the decoded body.

name: createNetworkFault
description:
Builds a `NET_*` `PreflightFault`, choosing the code from the shape of `cause`.

`response` is `undefined` until the transport has metadata to report. The
cause is kept as `cause`.

- `NET_ABORTED` when {@link isAbortCause} recognizes an abort-branded `Error`
  (including `ERR_ABORTED` from another Core copy) or a `DOMException` named
  `AbortError`. The message is `Request was aborted`.
- `NET_TIMEOUT` when {@link isTimeoutCause} recognizes a timeout-branded
  `Error` (including `ERR_TIMEOUT` from another Core copy) or a `DOMException`
  or `Error` named `TimeoutError`. The message is the cause's message, or
  `Request timed out` when that is empty.
- `NET_UNREACHABLE` for anything else, with the cause's message.

parameters.name: cause
parameters.description: Underlying cancellation, timeout, or transport failure.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: Transport metadata. `undefined` until that metadata exists.

name: createPreflightFault
description:
Builds a fault for a failure that may have happened before any response existed.

When `cause` is given, its message becomes the fault message; otherwise the
code is the message. The result is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault` with
`code`. `response` is `undefined` until transport metadata exists.

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: The specific failure.

parameters.name: cause
parameters.description: Underlying value, when there is one; the code becomes the message otherwise.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: Transport metadata. `undefined` until that metadata exists.

name: createUndecodedHttpStatusFault
description:
Builds an `HTTP_STATUS` fault for a non-2xx response that was never decoded, because the endpoint declared no `error` struct.

The fault is a native `Error` named `DefjsFault` with `code: 'HTTP_STATUS'`,
`data: undefined`, `status` copied from the response, and `response` as passed.

Use {@link createHttpStatusFault} when the body was decoded.

parameters.name: response
parameters.description: Metadata of the response; no body was read.

name: isAbortCause
description:
Whether `cause` is caller cancellation, across Core copies and platform abort errors.

Returns `true` for an `Error` carrying the non-enumerable
`Symbol.for('defjs.cause.aborted')` brand, including `ERR_ABORTED` from
another Core copy, or a `DOMException` named `AbortError`. An ordinary
unbranded `Error` with that name does not match. Other values return `false`.

Pass the underlying `fault.cause`; this function does not unwrap faults.
`createNetworkFault` uses this check to select `NET_ABORTED`. OpenTelemetry
uses it to treat caller cancellation as no failure while preserving timeouts as failures.

overloads.signature: function isAbortCause(cause: unknown): boolean;

name: isTimeoutCause
description:
Whether `cause` is a timeout, across Core copies and platform timeout errors.

Returns `true` for an `Error` carrying the non-enumerable

description:
Options for basic-auth interceptors, including a custom credential encoder.

`encode` replaces only the credential encoder. The default is
``btoa(`${username}:${password}`)``. The interceptor always prefixes the
returned string with `Basic `, so return the credential part alone: returning
`'Basic abc'` produces the header `Basic Basic abc`.

Accepted by {@link basicAuthHttpInterceptor} and {@link basicAuthSSEInterceptor}.

name: BulkheadOverflowError
description:
Cause attached to `EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED` when {@link concurrencyLimitHttpInterceptor}
rejects a request because its queue is full (`maxQueue` reached).

`name` is `'BulkheadOverflowError'`. The error carries the saturated bucket
`key`, `maxConcurrency`, and `maxQueue` for diagnostics and logging.

typeTable.description: Configured maximum queue length for the bucket.

name: ConcurrencyLimitInterceptorOptions
description:
Options for {@link concurrencyLimitHttpInterceptor}.

`maxConcurrency` caps the number of in-flight HTTP attempts allowed at once
per bucket. Requests beyond that limit wait in FIFO order up to `maxQueue`
(which defaults to `Infinity`), or fail immediately with
`EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED` carrying a {@link BulkheadOverflowError} as `cause`
when the queue is full.

`key` partitions limits across independent buckets (for example per selected
origin via `req.baseEndpoint ?? ""`, or by `req.method`). By default all
requests share one bucket (`""`).

typeTable.description: Maximum number of concurrent in-flight HTTP attempts per bucket; must be a positive integer (`>= 1`).

typeTable.name: maxQueue
typeTable.description: Maximum number of waiters allowed in the FIFO queue per bucket (`0` rejects immediately when busy); defaults to `Infinity`.

typeTable.description: Partitions concurrency and queue budgets into named buckets; defaults to one shared bucket (`""`).

name: HttpInterceptor
description:
Tagged HTTP interceptor accepted by client interceptor options.

Created by `createHttpInterceptor`. `kind` is the discriminant that lets
`withInterceptors` accept every interceptor kind in one list; only `kind: 'http'`
interceptors run for HTTP operations.

name: HttpInterceptorNext
description:
Continuation that runs the rest of the HTTP interceptor chain, or the handler.

`next(req)` only goes inward: the interceptors registered after this one, then
the Fetch handler. It is not a new operation call from outside the chain.
Call `next` again for a safe
replay (for example one 401 refresh) from the same interceptor; outer layers
do not run a second time. Once the chain has settled, calling `next` rejects
with `HTTP interceptor next() cannot be called after the chain has settled`.

Controls which header name is set, which HTTP methods receive the key, how
keys are generated, and whether caller-supplied headers are preserved.

name: Interceptor
description:
Any tagged interceptor accepted by client interceptor options.

`kind` (`'http'`, `'sse'`, `'web-socket'`, or `'operation'`) selects which operations an
interceptor runs for. `withInterceptors` accepts any mix; each transport runs
only its own kind, in registration order, and every operation runs the `'operation'` kind around it.

type Interceptor =
  | HttpInterceptor
  | SSEInterceptor
  | WebSocketInterceptor
  | OperationInterceptor;

name: InterceptorFn
description:
HTTP interceptor function: may inspect or modify the request, then call `next`.

Call `next(req)` or short-circuit with `makeResponse`. Wrap it with
`createHttpInterceptor` to register it.

name: OperationCall
description:
The operation call an operation interceptor wraps, described by its definition.

`transport` is `'http'`, `'sse'`, or `'websocket'`. `method` is the defined method; a WebSocket operation reports
`GET`, the method of its opening handshake. `path` is the defined path template, such as `/orders/:id`, before any
input is placed. `meta` is the definition's `meta`, the same read-only object every call shares. The input, the
request options, and the request itself are not part of it: the call has not been built when the interceptor runs.

Each definition reuses one record for all of its calls.

name: OperationInterceptor
description:
Tagged operation interceptor accepted by client interceptor options.

Created by `createOperationInterceptor`. Operation interceptors run for every HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket operation, in
registration order, outside the transport interceptors.

name: OperationInterceptorFn
description:
Operation interceptor function: observes one operation call from its start to the tuple it resolves with.

`next()` runs the whole call: input validation, the endpoint pick, the builder, every attempt with its interceptor
chain and retries, and the response decoding. It takes no arguments, so the interceptor cannot change the call. A
second call of `next()` returns the same promise and does not run the call again. The function is generic in the
result, so it can only resolve with what `next()` resolved with.

Code that the function runs inside `next()`, such as an OpenTelemetry `context.with`, is in effect for the whole
call, including the transport interceptors. `next()` never rejects. If the function throws or rejects, its layer
resolves with `EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED` and the thrown value as `cause`: that is what the operation resolves with,
and what `next()` resolves with in the operation interceptors registered before it. A stream or session the call
had already opened is closed with that value.

name: OperationResult
description:
The error-first tuple any operation resolves with, as an operation interceptor reads it.

Its first element is the fault, or `null` on success. The rest is the operation's own result: the data and response
for HTTP, the stream and its open information for SSE, the session and its connection for WebSocket.

name: SSEHandler
description:
Terminal `next` function an SSE interceptor receives; it opens an event stream for the request.

`next(req)` goes inward only: through the interceptors registered after this
one, then the transport that opens the stream. Calling it after the chain has
settled rejects.

`EventStreamHandle` extends `AsyncDisposable`. A short-circuit implementation
that builds its own handle must provide
`[Symbol.asyncDispose](): PromiseLike<void>` and connect it to the same close
lifecycle.

name: SSEInterceptor
description:
Tagged SSE interceptor for client option lists, accepted by `withInterceptors`.

Created by `createSSEInterceptor`. The `kind` tag lets `withInterceptors`
accept every interceptor kind in one list; only `kind: 'sse'`
interceptors run for SSE operations.

name: SSEInterceptorFn
description:
SSE interceptor function: may inspect, modify, or replace the request, then call `next`.

Call `next` (an {@link SSEHandler}) to continue the chain, or return your own
`EventStreamHandle` to short-circuit. Wrap it with `createSSEInterceptor` to
register it through `withInterceptors`.

A short-circuit handle must provide
`[Symbol.asyncDispose](): PromiseLike<void>` and connect it to the same close
lifecycle.

name: WebSocketHandler
description:
Terminal `next` function a WebSocket interceptor receives; it opens a session for the request.

`next(req)` goes inward only: through the interceptors registered after this
one, then the transport that opens the session. It resolves to a
{@link WebSocketSessionLike}. It may be called once per execute; a second
call, or a call after the chain has settled, rejects.

name: WebSocketInterceptor
description:
Tagged WebSocket interceptor for client option lists, accepted by `withInterceptors`.

Created by `createWebSocketInterceptor`. The `kind` tag lets
`withInterceptors` accept every interceptor kind in one list;
only `kind: 'web-socket'` interceptors run for WebSocket operations.

name: WebSocketInterceptorFn
description:
WebSocket interceptor function: may inspect, modify, or replace the request, then call `next`.

Call `next` (a {@link WebSocketHandler}) to continue the chain, or return your own
{@link WebSocketSessionLike} to short-circuit. Wrap it with
`createWebSocketInterceptor` to register it through `withInterceptors`.

The chain runs once per operation. Reconnects happen inside the session it
returns and do not run it again.

returning an unrelated resolved promise is not sufficient.

name: basicAuthHttpInterceptor
description:
HTTP interceptor that sets an `Authorization: Basic …` header from credentials.

It sets `Authorization: Basic <encoded>` on a copy of the request headers,
replacing any existing `Authorization` header. The default encoder is
``btoa(`${username}:${password}`)``, so credentials must be Latin-1. Without
`encode`, calling `basicAuthHttpInterceptor` throws
`Error: BasicAuthInterceptor is not supported in this environment` when `btoa`
is not available in the runtime. Use {@link basicAuthSSEInterceptor} for SSE
operations.

parameters.description: Factory returning username/password for each request.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Optional custom encoder (defaults to `btoa`).

name: basicAuthSSEInterceptor
description:
SSE interceptor that sets an `Authorization: Basic …` header from credentials.

It sets `Authorization: Basic <encoded>` on a copy of the request headers,
replacing any existing `Authorization` header. Encoding and the `btoa`
requirement are the same as for {@link basicAuthHttpInterceptor}, including
the synchronous throw when `btoa` is missing.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Factory returning username/password for each request.

parameters.name: options

name: concurrencyLimitHttpInterceptor
description:
HTTP interceptor that caps concurrent in-flight HTTP attempts per bucket.

When `maxConcurrency` requests are already active in a bucket, further
requests wait in FIFO order until a slot frees or `req.signal` aborts. While
waiting in the queue, transport `attemptTimeoutMs` and balancer pending-load
tracking have not started yet, and permits are released during `withRetry`
backoff waits so retries cannot deadlock the bulkhead.

- Pre-aborted or mid-queue aborted requests do not consume a permit and fail
  with `NET_ABORTED` or `NET_TIMEOUT`.
- Requests that exceed `maxQueue` reject with {@link BulkheadOverflowError},
  which Defjs reports as `EXT_INTERCEPTOR_FAILED` (`attempt.info` stays
  `{ attempted: false }`, so balancers do not eject endpoints and retries stop).
- `maxConcurrency` must be an integer `>= 1` and `maxQueue` an integer `>= 0`
  or `Infinity`; invalid values throw `RangeError` synchronously.

parameters.name: options
parameters.description: Concurrency cap, optional queue limit, and optional bucket key selector.

name: createHttpInterceptor
description:
Wraps an `InterceptorFn` as a tagged `HttpInterceptor`.

Returns `{ kind: 'http', fn }`. Call `next(req)` (optionally with a modified
request) or short-circuit with `makeResponse`. `next` runs only the
interceptors registered after this one and then the fetch handler. HTTP
interceptors do not run for SSE or WebSocket operations.

A deterministic URL error from `next(req)` rejects the returned promise, so
`.then` or `.catch` recovery runs; if it is not recovered, the operation
still reports `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: HTTP interceptor function.

name: createOperationInterceptor
description:
Wraps an `OperationInterceptorFn` as a tagged `OperationInterceptor`.

Returns `{ kind: 'operation', fn }`. An operation interceptor sees each operation call once, from the moment it is
called until it resolves its error-first tuple, so it observes what the transport interceptors cannot: an input
that fails validation (`REQ_INPUT_INVALID`), a builder or endpoint failure before any request exists
(`REQ_BUILD_FAILED`), the retries of one call, and a response that fails decoding after the transport chain
returned it (`HTTP_STATUS`, `RES_*`). For SSE and WebSocket the call resolves once the stream or session is open;
what happens on it later is observed through its `closed`.

It observes; it does not alter the call. Use a transport interceptor to change requests or responses.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: Operation interceptor function.

name: createSSEInterceptor
description:

Returns `{ kind: 'sse', fn }`. SSE interceptors run only for SSE operations, in
registration order; `next(req)` opens the stream through the remaining
interceptors.

A deterministic URL error from `next(req)` rejects the returned promise, so
`.then` or `.catch` recovery runs; if it is not recovered, the operation
still reports `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`.

`EventStreamHandle` extends `AsyncDisposable`. A structural short-circuit
implementation must provide `[Symbol.asyncDispose](): PromiseLike<void>` and
connect it to the same close lifecycle.

overloads.signature: function createSSEInterceptor(fn: SSEInterceptorFn): SSEInterceptor;

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: SSE interceptor function.

name: createWebSocketInterceptor
description:
Wraps a `WebSocketInterceptorFn` as a tagged `WebSocketInterceptor`.

Returns `{ kind: 'web-socket', fn }`. WebSocket interceptors run only for
WebSocket operations. `next` and the interceptor return a
{@link WebSocketSessionLike}, the interceptor-facing session. A wrapper or
short-circuit session must forward its `[Symbol.asyncDispose]()` teardown.

parameters.name: fn
parameters.description: WebSocket interceptor function.

name: idempotencyKeyHttpInterceptor
description:
HTTP interceptor that attaches an idempotency key header to mutating requests.

For requests whose method matches `methods` (default `POST` and `PATCH`),
clones `req.headers` and sets `headerName` (default `'Idempotency-Key'`).
When `respectExisting` is `true` (default) and the request already carries
`headerName`, the request passes through unchanged.

Without a custom `generate` callback, reuses `req.correlationId` so every
`withRetry` attempt of the same call sends the same idempotency key without
storing keys across calls. With a custom `generate` callback, memoizes
generated values by `req.correlationId` in a bounded LRU cache (4,096
entries) so custom generators are likewise called once per retry chain.

parameters.description: Optional header name, target methods, generator, and overwrite flag.

name: StructError
description:
Error returned by a failed struct parse, aggregating one or more {@link StructIssue}s and their formatters.

`name` is `'StructError'`. Construct it with `constructor(issues: StructIssue[])`. `issues` is the `readonly` list of those issues. `message` is the issue's message for a single issue, `N struct issues: <first message>` for several, and `Struct parse failed` for none.

Default issue messages name the received kind and omit the value, so `message` and `prettify()` can be logged. For example, `Expected number at id, received string`. `message` and the formatters use that text. The raw value stays on `StructIssue.received`; custom `errorMap` text is used verbatim and can reintroduce sensitive values.

Use `format()`, `flatten()`, or `prettify()` to present issues to callers.

- `struct.parse` stops at the first failure, so `issues` holds one {@link StructIssue} there.

- `format()` returns a {@link FormattedStructError} tree. Each node has an `_errors` array, and nested keys follow `issue.path`.

- `flatten()` returns a {@link FlattenedStructError}: messages with an empty path go to `formErrors`, the others are grouped by the first path segment in `fieldErrors`.

- `prettify()` returns one `× path: message` line per issue. An empty path is shown as `<root>`.

- `expected` describes the expected type or value.

- `message` is the final text, after an optional {@link ErrorMap} rewrite.

- `path` runs from the parse root to the failing location: field names and array indices. It is empty for a root-level failure.

- `received` is the value that failed at `path`.

`_struct` exists only in the type system. Structs have no `_struct` property at runtime, and a plain object with that type is not a valid struct. `input` and `output` are the phantom types. `optionalOut` is `true` when the third type argument is `true`, and `undefined` otherwise.

name: struct
description:
Facade object for building protocol-boundary structs and parsing values with its constructors and `struct.parse`.

Prefer this object over importing the constructor functions one by one. Compose shapes with
`struct.object`, then parse with `struct.parse` or let HTTP/SSE/WebSocket
endpoints apply the same contracts at the wire boundary. `struct` is a plain object of helpers.

### Primitives and containers

| Helper                                                                           | Role                                                      |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.string}()                                     | Text                                                      |
| {@link struct.number}()                                     | Number, `NaN` rejected                                    |
| {@link struct.boolean}()                                   | Boolean                                                   |
| {@link struct.bigint}()                                     | `bigint`, or a string that parses as one                  |
| {@link struct.date}()                                         | `Date`, from a `Date`, timestamp, or string               |
| {@link struct.literal}(value)                              | Exact literal                                             |
| {@link struct.null}()                                         | Only `null`                                               |
| {@link struct.any}() / unknown() ({@link struct.unknown}) | Any value except `null` and `undefined`                   |
| {@link struct.array}(item)                                   | Array of one item struct                                  |
| {@link struct.tuple}(items)                                  | Fixed-length array; `items` is one array of structs       |
| {@link struct.record}(value)                                | Plain object with string keys and one value struct        |
| {@link struct.object}(shape)                                | Plain object with fixed fields; unknown keys are stripped |
| {@link struct.or}(...options)                                   | First matching option                                     |
| {@link struct.intersection}(...structs)               | Every struct must match; object results are merged        |
| {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}(tag, options) | Object option picked by the value of the `tag` field      |
| {@link struct.enum}(values)                                   | String array, or the values of a `{ Name: value }` object |

### Body codecs and binary values

| Helper                                                                                                                         | Role                                                                                                        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| {@link struct.formData}(shape) / urlencoded(shape) ({@link struct.urlencoded})                     | Object struct plus a codec tag. The tag applies only when that value is the request body root               |
| {@link struct.arrayBuffer}() / blob() ({@link struct.blob}) / file() ({@link struct.file}) | Binary values. As a body root they are sent as bytes; as `output` / `error` they select that representation |
| {@link struct.string}()                                                                                   | Text. As a body root or an inbound `string` struct, the bytes stay text                                     |

### Parsing and modifiers

{@link struct.parse}(struct, value, options?) parses an unknown value and returns `[null, value]` or `[err, undefined]` where `err` is a `StructError`.

Every struct has the chainable modifiers `.optional()`, `.null()` / `.nullable()`, `.nullish()`, and `.alias(name)`. See {@link StructMethods}.

tags.name: example

typeTable.name: any
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts any value except null and undefined, without validation.

The value is returned unchanged, and nothing inside it is validated or stripped.

- Chain `.null()`, `.optional()`, or `.nullish()` to accept `null` or `undefined`.

- The output type is `any`. Prefer {@link struct.unknown}() when the caller should narrow the value.

typeTable.name: array
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses an array with one item struct.

- Parses every element with `item` and outputs a new array. A non-array fails with `invalid_type` (expected `array`).

- Parsing stops at the first failing element, and `issue.path` holds its index.

The result is an {@link ArrayStruct}, a `Struct<StructInput<S>[], Infer<S>[]>`.

typeTable.name: arrayBuffer
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts an ArrayBuffer.

- Accepts an `ArrayBuffer` only. Typed arrays and other views fail with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as bytes with `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as an `ArrayBuffer`.

typeTable.name: bigint
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a bigint or a bigint string and outputs a bigint.

- Accepts a `bigint`, or a string that `BigInt()` can parse. A `number` is rejected.

- Output is always a `bigint`; an unparsable string fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes a decimal string.

typeTable.name: blob
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Blob.

- Accepts a `Blob` (a `File` is a `Blob`). Anything else fails with `invalid_type`.

- As a body root it is sent as is, with the blob's own type or `application/octet-stream`.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as a `Blob`.

typeTable.name: boolean
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts boolean values.

Accepts `true` and `false` only. Other values, including `'true'` and `1`, fail with `invalid_type`.

typeTable.name: date
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a Date, timestamp, or date string and outputs a Date.

- Accepts a `Date`, a millisecond timestamp, or a string. A valid `Date` is returned as the same object. A number or string is converted with `new Date(value)`.

- Output is a `Date`. A value that produces an invalid date fails with `invalid_type`.

- When encoded for the wire, the value becomes an ISO 8601 string (`toISOString()`).

typeTable.name: discriminatedUnion
typeTable.description:
Struct that picks one object struct by the value of a tag field.

```ts
const Event = struct.discriminatedUnion("kind", [
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("created"), id: struct.number() }),
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("deleted"), id: struct.number() }),
]);
```

- Every option must be an object struct whose `discriminator` field is a required {@link struct.literal}(). The type check rejects an option that is not an object struct, has no such field, or has an optional or nullable one. A field that is not a literal struct (a `struct.string()`, say) or a tag value that two options share throws `TypeError` when the struct is created, and the message names the option index.

- The input must be a plain object. The tag value selects the option, and that option parses the whole object.

- A missing tag fails with `missing_key`, and an unknown tag fails with `invalid_union`. Both report the tag field's path. Other failures come from the selected option.

- With `struct.parse(..., { aliases: true })` the tag is read from the field's alias.

The result is a {@link DiscriminatedUnionStruct}. `RequiredDiscriminatorOptions` is not exported.
typeTable.type: <const TDiscriminator extends string, const TOptions extends readonly [ObjectStruct<ObjectShape>, ...ObjectStruct<ObjectShape>[]]>(discriminator: TDiscriminator, options: TOptions & RequiredDiscriminatorOptions<TDiscriminator, TOptions>) => DiscriminatedUnionStruct<TOptions>

typeTable.name: enum
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts one value from a list of strings or from the values of an object.

- With a non-empty string array, the accepted values are the array items.

- With an object, the accepted values are the object's string and number **values**, not its keys. `{ A: 'a', B: 2 }` accepts `'a'` and `2`.

- A TypeScript numeric `enum` object also accepts its member names, because the reverse mapping is part of its values.

- A value outside the set fails with `invalid_enum`. An object with no string or number value throws `TypeError` when the struct is created.

typeTable.name: file
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts a File.

- Accepts a `File` only; a plain `Blob` fails with `invalid_type`.

- Use it for a field of {@link struct.formData}(), or for a raw file body.

- As an `output` or `error` struct it makes the response body be read as a blob.

typeTable.name: formData
typeTable.description:
Object struct that is encoded as multipart FormData when it is the request body.

Parses like {@link struct.object}(), and carries a `formData` codec tag.

- The tag applies only when this struct's value is the request body root. The body is then sent as `FormData` with a platform multipart boundary.

- Arrays repeat the field name, `undefined` fields are skipped, and `Blob` / `File` values are appended as files. A nested object fails the request with `REQ_BUILD_FAILED`.

- `struct.parse` ignores the tag. It does not accept a `FormData` instance, only a plain object.

typeTable.name: intersection
typeTable.description:
Struct that requires a value to satisfy every given struct.

`struct.intersection` is variadic: pass each struct as its own argument.

- Parses the input with every struct and merges the results.

- When every struct is an object struct, the output is one object with the fields of all of them. Keys that none of them declares are removed.

- When two structs produce incompatible values for the same key, it fails with `invalid_intersection`.

- Accepts `null` only when every struct accepts it, including a nested intersection marked `.null()`.

- A single struct is returned unchanged, so it keeps its own identity and type, including `.optional()` and `.null()`.

- A nonempty variadic tuple must account for that singleton. Spreading a tuple that may contain only one member infers both the singleton and multi-member results. Its object fields may therefore be optional. A tuple known to contain at least two members keeps the required intersection semantics.

The result is an {@link IntersectionStruct}, a `Struct` whose input and output are the intersections of the member types.

typeTable.name: literal
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts exactly one boolean, null, number, or string value.

- Accepts only `value`. The comparison uses `Object.is`, so any other value fails with `invalid_literal`.

- `value` must be a `boolean`, `null`, `number`, or `string`.

- Use it for the tag field of {@link struct.discriminatedUnion}().
typeTable.type: <const T extends LiteralValue>(value: T) => Struct<T, T>

typeTable.name: null
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts only null.

Accepts `null` only. Every other value fails with `invalid_type`. That includes `undefined` at the root or in an array or tuple; a missing object or record field reports `missing_key` instead.

This is not the `.null()` modifier. The modifier adds `null` to the values another struct accepts.

typeTable.name: number
typeTable.description:
Struct that accepts number values except NaN.

- Accepts `number` values, including `Infinity`. `NaN` and non-numbers fail with `invalid_type`.

- Strings are not coerced.

typeTable.name: object
typeTable.description:
Struct that parses a plain object with a fixed set of fields.

`shape` maps field names to structs.

- Every field is **required** by default. A missing key fails with `missing_key`.

- `.optional()` and `.nullish()` allow a missing key. An absent optional field stays absent in the output.

- `.null()` / `.nullable()` allow `null`.

- `.alias(name)` sets the field's wire key. `struct.parse` reads logical keys by default; `{ aliases: true }` and HTTP JSON decoding read wire keys, and HTTP JSON encoding writes them. Parsed output uses logical keys.

- Keys that are not in `shape` are removed from the output. The output is a new object with a `null` prototype.

name: struct.discriminatedUnion
description:
Struct that picks one object struct by the value of a tag field.

```ts
const Event = struct.discriminatedUnion("kind", [
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("created"), id: struct.number() }),
  struct.object({ kind: struct.literal("deleted"), id: struct.number() }),
]);
```

description:

name: struct.intersection
description:
Struct that requires a value to satisfy every given struct.

`struct.intersection` is variadic: pass each struct as its own argument.

- Parses the input with every struct and merges the results.

- When every struct is an object struct, the output is one object with the fields of all of them. Keys that none of them declares are removed.

- When two structs produce incompatible values for the same key, it fails with `invalid_intersection`.

- Accepts `null` only when every struct accepts it, including a nested intersection marked `.null()`.

- A single struct is returned unchanged, so it keeps its own identity and type, including `.optional()` and `.null()`.

- A nonempty variadic tuple must account for that singleton. Spreading a tuple that may contain only one member infers both the singleton and multi-member results. Its object fields may therefore be optional. A tuple known to contain at least two members keeps the required intersection semantics.

The result is an {@link IntersectionStruct}, a `Struct` whose input and output are the intersections of the member types.

description:

Returns a pooled error-first tuple `[err, results, responses]`. On success,

order. On the first operation fault, already-started sibling calls are

`options.signal` or a derived `client({ signal })` takes precedence as

operation's exact success value and response metadata types. Rejects
zero-argument operations at compile time; pass operations that accept a
required or optional input. Use {@link concurrentMapSettled} when partial
results should be kept.

description:

`cookieName` defaults to `XSRF-TOKEN` and `headerName` to `X-XSRF-TOKEN` when omitted.
The token is read from `document.cookie`. An empty value means no header.
A token from another source is set with an interceptor.

typeTable.description: Request header name that receives the token. Must be a valid HTTP header name (an RFC 9110 token). A browser silently drops a name that Fetch forbids, such as `Cookie`, `Origin`, or a `Sec-` or `Proxy-` name, so the token is not sent. Defaults to `X-XSRF-TOKEN`.

name: withXSRF
description:
Enables XSRF cookie-to-header forwarding for browser HTTP requests.

Import this from `@defjs/core/xsrf`. Calling it checks `globalThis` immediately and
throws when `location` or `document` is missing, including in a Worker. Isomorphic
code adds this option only in the browser. It sets `config.finalizeHeaders`, which the
HTTP transport calls once per attempt. The hook receives the outgoing headers after
interceptors and before the default `Accept` is filled in, plus the resolved URL.
SSE and WebSocket requests do not get the header.
`cookieName` defaults to `XSRF-TOKEN` and `headerName` to `X-XSRF-TOKEN` when names
are omitted.

- The header is set only when all of these hold: the method is not `GET`, `HEAD`, `OPTIONS`, or `TRACE`; the request does not already have that header; `url.origin` equals the page origin; and `document.cookie` holds a non-empty token. A cross-origin request does not read the cookie.
- A throw while reading the cookie counts as no token. An empty token does not set the header.
- The origin check covers the URL the library builds. Fetch follows redirects itself, and after a redirect to another origin it removes only `Authorization`, so this header goes along. The target receives the token when it allows the header in its CORS preflight. To refuse that, pass {@link withHTTPHandle} a function that calls `fetch(new Request(request, { mode: "same-origin" }))` for requests to the page origin that carry the header. Do not apply that mode to a cross-origin API whose header comes from an interceptor: Fetch rejects any request to another origin in that mode. Such a request fails with `NET_UNREACHABLE` when a redirect leaves the origin and still follows a same-origin redirect. With `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer`, Fetch sends `Origin: null` for a same-origin POST in that mode, where the default mode sends the serialized origin, so a server that checks `Origin` can reject it. Some engines implement this differently.
- An invalid `headerName`, or a decoded cookie value that is not a valid header value (it holds CR, LF, or NUL in the middle, or a code point above U+00FF), fails that call with `EXT_HOOK_FAILED`. The `cause` is the `TypeError` the platform threw, and no request is sent. Safe methods are not affected.
- A token from another source is set with an interceptor.

Always call `useClient(explicitClient)` at the top level of a component or custom Hook, even with an explicit client; not in an ordinary function or event callback. Do not write `explicitClient ?? useClient()`, which conditionally calls a Hook. The override does not write Context or create a provider, and the Hook still subscribes to Context.

The returned value is the exact `DerivableClient` that was supplied. Call it with request options at the call site to derive a `Client` value for one call: `getOrder(client({ signal }), input)`. It is a function, so do not pass it to `useState` or a state setter: React calls a function argument as a lazy initializer or an updater. Does not create, cache, or dispose the client — pass the client returned by `createClient`. Installing it calls `app.provide(HTTP_CLIENT, client)`, so components read the client with `injectClient()`. The client is stored as given: it is not wrapped in `ref`, `reactive`, or `markRaw`.

name: injectClient
description:
Vue composable that injects the Defjs client for a key, defaulting to {@link HTTP_CLIENT}.

`injectClient(key)` reads the nearest provider for that key; omitted or `undefined` uses `HTTP_CLIENT`. Call in a valid Vue injection context: synchronous `setup()`, compiler-restored `<script setup>` after top-level `await`, or a synchronous `app.runWithContext()` callback (Vue 3.3+). `app.runWithContext()` supplies only synchronous app-level context, not subtree overrides or context across ordinary `await`.

For a custom `InjectionKey<DerivableClient>`, use `app.provide(key, client)` or an ancestor’s `provide(key, client)`. Share the same `Symbol` object; matching descriptions do not make keys equal. `createClientPlugin(client)` still takes only the client and provides `HTTP_CLIENT`.

It returns the exact client value provided for the selected key, and throws an `Error` without an active injection context or a client for the selected key. Installing the plugin alone does not establish an injection context.

The injected `DerivableClient` is a function. Call it with request options at the call site to derive a `Client` value for one call: `getOrder(client({ signal }), input)`. Do not pass it to `watch` or `computed` as the source: Vue calls a function source. Do not wrap it in `ref` or `reactive`. The provider holds only a root client; a derived `Client` value is not accepted, so create it where the operation is called.

If called outside a Vue injection context or no client was provided for
the requested key. A missing custom key does not fall back to `HTTP_CLIENT`.

name: OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions
description:
Options for the HTTP transport — the shared options with an HttpResponse in responseHook.

Set on `http` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, res, req)` receives the `HttpResponse` that came back through the interceptor, before the client decodes a declared body, together with the original `HttpRequest`. Read `req.meta` for application-defined request metadata; the span already carries each key as `defjs.meta.<key>`.

- Each attempt gets its own HTTP span, so a call that `withRetry` retries has one per attempt under the same operation span. The span ends as soon as `responseHook` returns; the hook is not awaited, so only its synchronous part can still change the span. A status of 400 or above ends it `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the status string; 100–399 leaves its status unset. A body that later fails to decode against the declared struct does not change this span; the operation span reports it. An asynchronous hook rejection after end is reported through `diag.error`; configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive it. It cannot append events to an ended span.

- A rejection through the interceptor has no response status and does not call `responseHook`. That includes a network failure, a timeout (`ERR_TIMEOUT`, or an abort whose reason is `TimeoutError`), caller cancellation, any declared-body read failure (`BodyFailure`, including text, blob, and bytes, not only JSON), a progress observer failure (`EXT_OBSERVER_FAILED`), and a request refused before it is sent (an invalid method, a URL with credentials, a header value the platform rejects, or a throwing `finalizeHeaders` hook), which carries the platform error or the hook's own error, not a library class. The span ends `ERROR` with `error.type` set to the thrown class name, such as `TypeError`, `Error` or `BodyFailure`, or to `timeout` for a timeout. Caller cancellation is the exception: the span records `http.aborted`, keeps its status unset and has no `error.type`, and the `http.client.request.duration` sample has none either. The HTTP span emits no log; the operation call logs a failure once.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip HTTP instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

overloads.signature:
type OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions =
  OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions<HttpResponse<unknown>>;

name: OpenTelemetryServerOptions
description:
Options for {@link withOpenTelemetryServer}: tracer, meter, logger, propagator, and per-transport settings.

Pass application-owned OpenTelemetry `Tracer`, `Meter`, and/or `Logger` handles.
This package does not initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK.

Every operation call is observed from the moment it is called until it resolves its error-first tuple, so input validation (`REQ_INPUT_INVALID`), a builder or endpoint failure (`REQ_BUILD_FAILED`), the retries of one call, and a response that fails decoding (`HTTP_STATUS`, `RES_*`) all reach telemetry. Under the operation, each HTTP attempt and each SSE or WebSocket connection is observed at the transport.

- `tracer` — Optional. Each operation call gets an `INTERNAL` span named `defjs.operation.name`: the HTTP method (`HTTP` for `_OTHER`), `SSE` or `WebSocket`, then the definition's path template, as in `GET /orders/:id`. It carries `defjs.operation.name` and the `defjs.meta.*` attributes, and on failure `error.type` set to the fault code with status `ERROR`. Caller cancellation (`NET_ABORTED`) adds the event `http.aborted`, `sse.aborted` or `websocket.aborted` and leaves the status unset. The span ends when the tuple resolves, so for SSE and WebSocket it covers startup only. Its child is one `CLIENT` span per HTTP attempt or per SSE or WebSocket connection. A call without an active parent span starts a new trace, as any OpenTelemetry span does; choose what is kept with the SDK's sampler. Without a tracer there are no local spans and no span hooks.

- `meter` — Optional. Records `defjs.client.operation.duration` (seconds, per operation call, with `defjs.operation.name` and, on failure, `error.type` set to the fault code) and the transport metrics. Without it no package metrics are recorded.

- `logger` — Optional. A `Logger` from `@opentelemetry/api-logs`, not a Winston/Pino Logger. A failed operation call emits one `WARN` LogRecord, `defjs.client.operation.exception`, with `defjs.operation.name`, `error.type` (the fault code), `exception.type` and the `defjs.meta.*` attributes, correlated with the operation span. An SSE stream or WebSocket session that fails after it opened emits one more on its transport event. Caller cancellation logs nothing. Without a logger no LogRecords are emitted. Defjs never obtains a global logger or owns its provider.

- `propagator` — Defaults to W3C Trace Context + Baggage.

- `includeErrorDiagnostics` — Defaults to `false`. With `true`, failures also export their error text: a failed span gets the error message as its status description, its `exception` events carry `exception.message` and `exception.stacktrace`, and failure logs carry `exception.message` and `exception.stacktrace`. For an operation call that is the fault's `message` and `stack`; a fault's message is often its cause's message, and platform error text can contain the request URL with its query. The cause chain and the enumerable fields of an error are never exported. This is not a redaction control: redact in an SDK processor if you need one.

- `http`, `sse`, `webSocket` — Per-transport options. Omitting a block leaves it unset and the transport enabled. A transport is disabled only by `{ enabled: false }`. `withOpenTelemetryServer` reads each present block once and copies its fields.

name: OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions
description:
Options for the SSE transport — the shared options with the stream handle in responseHook.

Set on `sse` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. It has no fields of its own: `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`.

- `responseHook(span, stream, req)` runs once the stream has opened, before the span records `sse.connected`. `stream` is the `EventStreamHandle` the transport returned; `req` is the original `HttpRequest`.

- SSE is traced at connection level. After startup the span stays open until `stream.closed` settles, and records `sse.connected`, then one of `sse.closed` (server EOF), `sse.aborted` (`stream.close()`, or a caller abort of the open stream or of the handshake whose reason is not `TimeoutError`; the span ends with its status unset and the connection metrics carry `defjs.result` `aborted`), or `sse.error` (including an abort whose reason is `TimeoutError`, which ends the span `ERROR` with `error.type` `timeout`). No per-event spans are created. Reconnects happen inside the transport without rerunning interceptors, so `url.full`, `server.address` and `server.port` describe the first connection even when a reconnect picks another endpoint.

- A non-2xx handshake is observed as a connection failure: the span ends `ERROR`. The operation call then fails and logs once; a failure after the stream opened logs once on the `defjs.client.sse.exception` event.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip SSE instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions
description:
Shared per-transport OpenTelemetry client options: whether the transport is enabled and its span hooks, generic over the response type.

`TResponse` is what `responseHook` receives: `HttpResponse<unknown>` for HTTP, `EventStreamHandle<unknown>` for SSE, `WebSocketSessionLike` for WebSocket. See {@link OpenTelemetryServerHttpOptions}, {@link OpenTelemetryServerSSEOptions} and {@link OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions}.

`enabled` defaults to `true`; only `enabled: false` turns the transport off.

Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied. `startSpanHook` runs synchronously before span creation for its own transport. Its attributes are applied after built-in attributes, so the application may override `url.full` or another initial value. If it throws, Defjs creates the span with built-in attributes and continues the request. `requestHook` runs after span creation and before the request is sent; `responseHook` runs after the transport result is returned. Both may return a promise, but neither is awaited: a throw or rejection never blocks or fails the operation. `responseHook` receives the original request as its third argument.

These options shape the transport span: one `CLIENT` span per HTTP attempt, or per SSE or WebSocket connection. It is a child of the operation span, which `withOpenTelemetryServer` creates for the whole operation call and which no hook reaches; see {@link OpenTelemetryServerOptions}.

While `span.isRecording()` is true, hook failures record `defjs.otel.hook.error` and `exception` events. The `exception` event carries only `exception.type` (the class name, not a Defjs fault code), and neither `exception.message` nor `exception.stacktrace` unless `includeErrorDiagnostics` is on, because runtime error text can include the full request URL or a response body fragment; the same rule applies to the `exception` event recorded when a transport fails. For non-recording spans (ended or unsampled), failures go to the OpenTelemetry diagnostic logger through `diag.error`. Applications must configure `diag.setLogger(...)` from `@opentelemetry/api` to receive them; there is no automatic output by default. The package does not initialize the SDK, and this diagnostic is not a separate SDK `LogRecord`.

Caller cancellation is not a failure, on every transport. An abort cause that is not a timeout (`ERR_ABORTED`, or an `AbortError`) leaves the span status unset, records no exception and no `error.type`, and adds the span event `http.aborted`, `sse.aborted` or `websocket.aborted`. The duration metrics are still recorded, without `error.type`; the connection metrics carry `defjs.result` `aborted`. A timeout (`ERR_TIMEOUT`, or a `TimeoutError` such as the reason of `AbortSignal.timeout()`) stays a failure: the span ends `ERROR` and `error.type` is `timeout`. There is no `timeout` option; a deadline is `signal`.

By default, `url.full` resolves only `request.endpoint` against optional `request.baseEndpoint`; `request.query` is not appended. That boundary is not query redaction. As the OpenTelemetry semantic conventions require, credentials in the endpoint's userinfo are replaced with `REDACTED:REDACTED`, and the values of the default sensitive query keys (`sig`, `Signature`, `AWSAccessKeyId`, `X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Amz-Credential`, `X-Amz-Security-Token`, `X-Goog-Signature`) are replaced with `REDACTED`, but the package has no other built-in redactor or sensitive-key policy. A `url.full` returned by `startSpanHook` is redacted the same way, but a URL an application writes through the `Span` object in `requestHook` or `responseHook` is not intercepted, so construct and, if needed, redact it explicitly.

Every span carries `http.request.method`, which is `GET` for the WebSocket handshake. A method outside RFC 9110, `PATCH` and `QUERY` is recorded as `_OTHER`, and a method that Fetch sends in upper case is recorded in upper case; `http.request.method_original` keeps the method as given when it differs.

name: OpenTelemetryServerWebSocketOptions
description:
Options for the WebSocket transport — the shared options plus queryPropagation.

Set on `webSocket` in `OpenTelemetryServerOptions`. `enabled`, `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook` come from `OpenTelemetryServerTransportOptions`; `responseHook(span, session, req)` receives the opened `WebSocketSessionLike` and the original `HttpRequest`.

`queryPropagation` defaults to `false`: the WebSocket query string is left unchanged and no trace context or baggage is written into the URL. Browser WebSocket clients usually cannot set headers, so enabling it writes the propagated context to the end of the query string, replacing any parameter of the same name. Query strings can be recorded by proxies, access logs and APM tools, and baggage values can be sensitive. Turn it on only after you accept that exposure.

WebSocket is traced at connection level. The span stays open until `session.closed` settles. It records `websocket.connected`, then `websocket.closed` for a normal close, `websocket.aborted` for a caller abort, or `websocket.error`. A close frame from the server counts as normal with any code, including 1011. An abrupt drop without a close frame (1006) ends the session in error and logs once on the `defjs.client.websocket.exception` event, on every runtime. A caller abort, of an open session or while the WebSocket is still connecting, ends the span with its status unset and no log, and the connection metrics carry `defjs.result` `aborted`. When the abort reason is `TimeoutError`, it is a connection failure instead: the span ends `ERROR` with `error.type` `timeout`, one log is emitted (by the operation call while connecting, on the connection event for an open session), and an open session also records `websocket.error`. No per-message spans are created. The span carries `http.request.method` `GET`, the method of the opening handshake. `url.full` uses the `ws:` or `wss:` form of the connection URL. As with SSE, connection attributes describe the first connection; a reconnect to another endpoint does not change them.

Pass `{ enabled: false }` to skip WebSocket instrumentation. Span hooks run only when a `tracer` is supplied.

name: withOpenTelemetryServer
description:
Client option that installs outbound OpenTelemetry interceptors for every operation call and for HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket.

Appends an operation interceptor when a `tracer`, `meter`, or `logger` is supplied, then one interceptor per enabled transport, in the order HTTP, SSE, WebSocket. Apply it at `createClient` time, once per client: every operation the client runs is observed through it. It does not initialize the OpenTelemetry SDK or acquire global tracer, meter, or logger handles: pass the ones your application owns. Each transport can be toggled or customized via `http`, `sse`, and `webSocket`.

`options` is required. It carries `tracer`, `meter`, `logger`, `propagator`, `includeErrorDiagnostics`, and the `http` / `sse` / `webSocket` transport options. Pass `{}` to install the interceptors with propagation only.

Each of `tracer`, `meter` and `logger` is optional and works without the others. Without `tracer`, the plugin creates no local spans, never calls `trace.getTracer(...)`, and skips `startSpanHook`, `requestHook` and `responseHook`. Propagation still forwards the extracted parent context.

HTTP, SSE, and WebSocket are on by default. Pass `{ enabled: false }` on a transport to skip it: its operations then produce no operation span, metric or log either.

`http`, `sse`, and `webSocket` are read once, in that order, during this call. A missing block stays missing. `tracer`, `meter`, `logger`, `propagator`, and hook functions keep their identity. Replacing a block, or changing its fields, after this call does not affect the returned option.

`enabled` is read next. Only `enabled: false` disables a block, and that branch does not read its hooks or `queryPropagation`. Otherwise the copy continues with `startSpanHook`, `requestHook`, and `responseHook`; a WebSocket block then copies `queryPropagation`. Those getters run here, once. If a getter throws, the exception leaves this call immediately and later blocks are not read. It is not caught or deferred until the option is applied.

The supplied Meter's instrument creation methods are called each time the returned option is applied to a client config, not during this call. The Meter/SDK controls instrument identity and aggregation. Each duration histogram receives its own copy of the default bucket boundaries.
